# Text
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad, together with the commentary composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya;
the Śikṣādhyāya:
From whom the entire world is born and into whom alone it is dissolved.
Salutation to that Self of Knowledge by whom this [world] is sustained.
(1) I perpetually bow down to those former teachers by whom all the Vedāntas were explained through the methods of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition. (2)
By the grace of my teacher, this commentary on the essence of the *Taittirīyaka* is being composed by me for those who desire its clear meaning. (3)

In the preceding section, the obligatory (*nitya*) rites were established for the purpose of exhausting accumulated demerit (*durita*), and the optional (*kāmya*) rites for those seeking specific fruits. Now, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is introduced for the purpose of abandoning the cause of the undertaking of karma. Desire (*kāma*) must be the cause of karma, because it is that which impels one to action. For those whose desires are fulfilled, the absence of desire results in abiding in their own Self (*svātman*); thus, activity is no longer possible. And when the Self is desired, there is the fulfillment of all desires. For the Self is indeed Brahman; the author will later declare that the knower of That attains the Supreme.

Therefore, liberation is the effortless abiding in one's own self upon the cessation of ignorance; for the scriptures state: "He finds fearlessness, he attains a firm foundation, he reaches this Self consisting of bliss," and so forth. Because there is no undertaking of optional or prohibited actions, because those already commenced are exhausted through experience, and because there is an absence of transgression due to the constant performance of obligatory duties, liberation is simply abiding in one's own self without effort.

Alternatively, if it is argued that liberation arises from karma alone because karma is the cause of that unsurpassed bliss denoted by the word "heaven" (svarga), we say no; for karma is manifold. Indeed, there exist numerous karmas performed in various previous births—some whose fruits have already begun to ripen and some whose fruits have not—which possess mutually contradictory results.

Therefore, since it is impossible for those [karmas] whose fruits have not yet begun to be exhausted through enjoyment in a single lifetime, there arises the commencement of a body caused by remaining karma, and the existence of a residue of karma is established. This is known from hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts (śruti and smṛti), such as: "Those who here have performed pleasant conduct, by that remainder... and so forth. If it is argued that the obligatory rites (nitya-karma) are intended for the exhaustion of uncommenced desirable and undesirable fruits, we say no; for it is heard in scripture that there is transgression (pratyavāya) in their non-performance.

For the word *pratyavāya* refers to that which is undesirable; since it is accepted that obligatory rites (*nitya*) are for the purpose of avoiding the future *pratyavāya*—which consists of suffering and is caused by the non-performance of what is obligatory—they are not for the purpose of exhausting karma whose fruit has not yet begun. Even if obligatory rites were for the purpose of exhausting karma whose fruit has not yet begun, they would exhaust only the impure [karma], not the pure, because there is no contradiction between them. Indeed, no contradiction with obligatory rites is possible in the case of karma that has a desirable fruit, because such karma is of a pure nature.

For a contradiction between the pure and the impure is logical. Furthermore, since there is no possibility of the cessation of desires—which are the causes of karma—in the absence of knowledge, the destruction of all karma is not established. For one who does not know the Self, desire exists because its objects are non-self fruits; yet desire for the Self itself is impossible, because it is eternally attained. And it has been stated that the Self is itself the Supreme Brahman. Moreover, the non-performance of obligatory duties (nitya-karma) is a mere non-existence; therefore, the arising of sin (pratyavāya) from such non-performance is untenable.

Therefore, since the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) is the defining characteristic of the transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from previously accumulated sins, there is no inconsistency in the use of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the phrase "one who does not perform the enjoined action" (*akurvan vihitam karma*). Otherwise, the arising of an entity from the absence of an entity would contradict all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, the claim that [the Self] abides in its own nature without effort is untenable.

As for the claim that because unsurpassed bliss, which is denoted by the word "heaven," is caused by ritual action (*karman*), liberation (*mokṣa*) must therefore begin from ritual action itself—that is not so, because liberation is eternal. For nothing eternal is ever produced in the world; whatever is produced is impermanent. Therefore, liberation is not something produced by ritual action. If it is argued that rituals, when conjoined with knowledge (*vidyā*), have the capacity to produce the eternal—that too is not so, because of contradiction. It is contradictory to say that something is both eternal and produced.

If it is argued that liberation is indeed something that begins—just like the non-existence resulting from destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva)—on the grounds that "whatever is destroyed never arises again," we say no; for liberation is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva). It is impossible for even the non-existence resulting from destruction to begin, because since non-existence lacks any specific qualities, this [claim] is a mere conceptual construction. For non-existence is the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) of existence.

For just as an entity, though non-different [in its essence], is distinguished by jars, cloths, and so forth—such that there is a "jar-entity" and a "cloth-entity," both being non-different [from existence]—so too is non-existence, though devoid of distinctions, conceptualized through its connection with action and qualities, just like substance and the rest. For non-existence does not coexist with qualifiers in the way a blue lotus or similar things do. If it were possessed of qualifiers, it would simply be an existent entity (*bhāva*). If it is argued that because the agent of knowledge and action is eternal, liberation—which is produced by the continuum of knowledge and action—is also eternal, we say no.

Because agency is of the nature of suffering—like the current of the Gaṅgā—and because liberation would be impossible if agency were to cease, it follows that liberation is abiding in one's own self upon the cessation of the causes of appropriation, namely ignorance, desire, and action. Since the Self itself is Brahman, and the cessation of ignorance occurs through the knowledge of That, the Upaniṣad is commenced for the purpose of the knowledge of Brahman.

"Upaniṣad" refers to knowledge. It is so called because it destroys or brings to an end the darkness of conception, birth, old age, and so forth for those who practice it; or because it leads one to the realization of Brahman; or because the supreme good is seated (*upaniṣanna*) within it. Since the book has that as its purpose, the text itself is also called "Upaniṣad."

Oṃ. May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutations to Brahman! Salutations to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.

Thus ends the first section in the Chapter on Training. (TaittU 1.1.1) May Mitra—the deity presiding over the function of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and over the day—be auspicious (*śam*) for us. Likewise, may Varuṇa—the deity presiding over the function of the in-breath (*apāna*) and over the night; Aryaman, who presides over the eye and the sun; Indra, over strength; Bṛhaspati, over speech and the intellect; and Viṣṇu of the wide stride (*urukrama*), whose step is vast, who presides over the two feet—may they all be auspicious for us. Thus are the deities with respect to the internal self (*adhyātma*). The phrase "may they be auspicious for us" is to be supplied everywhere.

For since those [qualities] which produce happiness will come about through the absence of obstacles to the hearing, retention, and application of knowledge, their status as producers of happiness is prayed for with the words, "May they be auspicious to us. By one who desires to know the knowledge of Brahman, the acts of salutation and the recitation of the Veda are performed with respect to Vāyu for the sake of pacifying obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman. Since all fruits of action depend upon him, Vāyu is Brahman; "to that Brahman, salutation (namaḥ). The completion of the sentence is: "I perform an act of prostration."

"Salutations to you, O Vāyu! I pay homage"—by these words, both indirect and direct, Vāyu alone is being addressed. Furthermore, since you alone, in relation to the eyes and other senses, are the external, proximate, unobstructed, and manifest Brahman, therefore I shall speak of you alone as the manifest Brahman. "Truth" (*ṛtam*)—the matter well-determined in the intellect according to the scriptures and according to what ought to be done—I shall speak of you alone, because that is dependent upon you.

"Truth" (*satyam*) is that very [principle] which is accomplished through speech and body; since even that is accomplished only by depending upon you, I shall speak of you alone as Truth. That Brahman, named Vāyu, who consists of all things and has been thus praised by me, may protect me by joining me with knowledge for those seeking knowledge. May that same Brahman protect the teacher, the speaker, by joining him with the capacity for speaking. The repetition—"May he protect me, may he protect the speaker"—is for the sake of showing reverence.
"Oṃ, peace, peace, peace"—this threefold utterance is for the purpose of pacifying the obstacles encountered in the acquisition of knowledge, whether they be internal, external, or celestial.
Thus ends the first section (anuvāka). // 1 //
Om. We shall explain phonetics (*śīkṣā*). Phoneme, accent, measure, strength, melody, and continuity—thus has the chapter on phonetics been declared. Thus ends the second recitation.

Since the Upaniṣads have as their primary purpose the knowledge of the meaning, the Śīkṣādhyāya is commenced so that there may be no cessation of effort in the recitation of the text. *Śikṣā* is that by which the phonemes and so forth are taught, characterized by the correct pronunciation of letters and the like; or, *śikṣā* refers to the phonemes and so forth themselves, as they are what are to be learned (*śikṣyante*). *Śīkṣā* is simply *śikṣā*; the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). We shall explain that *śīkṣā*, that is, we shall clearly and completely expound it. This form is derived from the root *cakṣiṅ*, which is replaced by *khyāñ* and preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*, signifying the object in its manifest state.

In this context, *varṇa* refers to the letters beginning with *a*; *svara* refers to the accents such as the acute (*udātta*); *mātrā* refers to the durations such as the short (*hrasva*); *bala* refers to the specific effort (*prayatna*) involved; *sāman* refers to the evenness or uniformity of pronunciation in the middle of the letters; and *santāna* means continuity, which is to say *saṃhitā*. This chapter, in which this subject matter to be learned (*śikṣitavya*)—namely, phonetics (*śikṣā*)—is taught, is thus called the "Chapter on Phonetics" (*śīkṣādhyāya*). The word "spoken" (*ukta*) serves as a concluding statement.
Thus ends the second section.

(May there be) glory for us both; may there be spiritual luster for us both. Now, therefore, we shall expound the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Saṃhitā, in five sections: concerning the worlds (*adhiloka*), concerning the luminaries (*adhijyautiṣa*), concerning knowledge (*adhividyā*), concerning progeny (*adhipraja*), and concerning the self (*adhyātma*). These they call the "Great Saṃhitās. Now, concerning the worlds: the earth is the prior form; the sky is the posterior form; space is the junction.

Now the *Saṃhitopaniṣad* is being expounded. In this regard, whatever fame may be obtained through the thorough knowledge of the *Saṃhitopaniṣad* and so forth, let that belong to both of us—the disciple and the teacher—equally. And let the splendor (*tejas*) of Brahmanic luster (*brahmavarcasa*) resulting from that also belong to us equally; such is the benediction (*āśis*) uttered by the disciple. For a prayer is appropriate for the disciple because he has not yet attained his goal, whereas it is not appropriate for the teacher, since he has already attained his goal. Indeed, it is the teacher who is called one who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtārtha*).

Now, immediately following this, we shall explain the *upaniṣad* of the *saṃhitā*—that is, the philosophical vision concerning the *saṃhitā*—which is closely connected to the present work. This is because the intellect, having been long cultivated by the preceding portion consisting of the rules for the characteristics of the *adhyāya*, cannot be suddenly introduced to the subject matter of understanding the meaning; therefore, [we proceed] with that which is proximate to the text. "In five topics" (*pañcasv adhikaraṇeṣu*) means in five bases, that is, in five objects of knowledge.

"What are they? he asks. [The answer is: "That which is the vision regarding the worlds (*adhiloka*)—that is, the vision concerning the worlds—is *adhiloka*. Likewise, there is *adhijyautiṣa*, *adhividyā*, *adhipraja*, and *adhyātma*. These five subjects of the Upaniṣads are called "Great Samhitās" by those who know the Veda, because their subject matter consists of great entities such as the worlds and so forth, and because they concern the *Saṃhitā*. Now, among those [Upaniṣads] as they have been introduced, the vision regarding the worlds (*adhiloka*) is being stated.

The word "atha" (then/now) is used everywhere for the purpose of indicating the sequence of the meditative visualization (*darśana*). "Earth" is the *pūrvarūpa* (prior form); *pūrvarūpa* means the prior letter. What is meant is that one should perform the visualization of the earth upon the prior letter of the *saṃhitā*. Likewise, "heaven" is the *uttararūpa* (subsequent form), and "space" is the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*). "Conjunction" (*sandhi*) is the middle, because the prior and subsequent forms are joined together (*sandhīyate*) within it.

"Vāyu is the connection"—thus with respect to the worlds (*adhiloka*). Now, with respect to the luminaries (*adhijyautiṣa*): "Agni is the prior form; Āditya is the subsequent form; the waters are the junction; lightning is the connection"—thus with respect to the luminaries. Now, with respect to knowledge (*adhividyā*): "The teacher is the prior form... (TaittU 1.3.2).

The pupil is the subsequent form; knowledge is the junction; the teaching is the connection. This is with respect to knowledge (*adhividyam*). Now, with respect to progeny (*adhiprajam*): the mother is the prior form; the father is the subsequent form; the offspring is the junction; procreation is the connection. This is with respect to progeny. (TaittU 1.3.3)

Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): the lower jaw is the prior form; the upper jaw is the subsequent form; speech is the junction; the tongue is the connection. This is with reference to the self. These are the great conjunctions (*mahāsaṃhitā*). He who knows these great conjunctions as thus explained is joined with offspring, with cattle, with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), with food, and with the heavenly world.
Thus ends the third section. 3.

And meditation (*upāsana*) is, according to the scriptures, a continuous succession of identical cognitions, unmixed with other cognitions, and having as its object the focal point prescribed by the scriptures. Furthermore, the meaning of the word "meditation" is well-established in common usage, as in "he meditates on the teacher" (*gurum upāste*) or "he meditates on the king" (*rājānam upāste*). For one who attends constantly upon the teacher and others is said to "meditate. And he obtains the fruit of that meditation. Therefore, here too, for one who knows thus, there is union with offspring and so forth, ending with heaven;
the meaning is that he attains the fruits such as offspring.

He who is the bull among the meters, possessing all forms, who was born from the nectar of the meters—may that Indra inspire me with wisdom. O God, may I become a bearer of the nectar of immortality. May my body be radiant; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my two ears. You are the treasury of the Veda, covered by wisdom; protect what I have heard. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 1.3.2–4; Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.4.1)

Bringing, spreading out, and quickly preparing for herself garments, cattle, food, and drink for me at all times—therefore, bring to me prosperity, together with woolly cattle; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) come hither; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge go forth; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge advance; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be self-controlled; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be tranquil; *svāhā*. May the students of sacred knowledge be perfectly calm; *svāhā*. (TaittU 1.4.2)

May I be glorious among the people, svāhā! May I be better than the wealthy, svāhā! O Bhaga, may I enter into you, svāhā! O Bhaga, do you enter into me, svāhā! In you, who have a thousand branches, O Bhaga, I cleanse myself, svāhā! Just as waters flow down a slope, just as months follow the aging of days, so may the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) come to me from every side, O Dhātṛ, svāhā! You are the neighbor; shine upon me, come to me, svāhā! Thus ends the fourth section (anuvāka). 4.

The recitation (*japa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) are prescribed as the means for attaining that [state] for one who desires wisdom (*medhā*) and one who desires prosperity (*śrī*), because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "May he, Indra, quicken me with wisdom; from that, bring me prosperity. That which is the "bull" (*ṛṣabha*) among the *chandasaḥ*, i.e., the Vedas, due to its preeminence—being "all-formed" (*viśvarūpa*) because it pervades all speech, as seen in another Vedic passage beginning, "Just as by a pin... and so forth—for this very reason, the syllable *oṃ* possesses the nature of a bull.

Since the syllable *oṃ* is indeed the object of worship here, its praise through words such as "the bull" (*ṛṣabha*) and so forth is entirely appropriate. From the *chandāṃsi*, that is, from the Vedas—for the Vedas are indeed immortality—from that immortality he was born. The meaning is that for Prajāpati, who was performing austerity and desired to grasp the most excellent essence from the worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and the *vyāhṛtis*, the syllable *oṃ* appeared as that most excellent essence; for the production of the eternal *oṃ* cannot be conceived in a literal sense.

May that very *oṃkāra*, who is Indra, the lord of all desires and the Supreme Lord, satisfy (*spṛṇotu*)—that is, gladden or strengthen—me with wisdom (*medhayā*), that is, with discernment (*prajñayā*). For the strength of wisdom is what is sought; for he is the one entitled to the knowledge of Brahman, which is the cause of immortality (*amṛtasya*). O God, may I become a "holder" (*dhāraṇaḥ*), a sustainer. Furthermore, may my body be "far-seeing" (*vicarṣaṇam*), meaning wise and fit for its purpose. The verb "may it be" (*bhūyāt*) is thus transformed from the third person to the first person.

"May my tongue be most honeyed"—that is to say, exceedingly sweet in speech. "From both ears, through the two organs of hearing, may I hear much"—that is to say, "may I become a great listener. The meaning of the sentence is: "May this aggregate of causes and effects be fit for the knowledge of the Self," for it is for that very purpose that wisdom (*medhā*) is prayed for. "Thou art the sheath of Brahman," the Supreme Self, because [the Self] is the substratum of perception, just like a sword [is perceived within its scabbard].

For you are the image of Brahman; in you, Brahman is perceived. You are "covered" (pihita)—that is, veiled—by *medhā*, meaning by worldly intelligence; the sense is that your true nature is unknown to those of ordinary intellect. "Protect my *śruta*"—meaning the knowledge of the Self and so forth, preceded by hearing (*śravaṇa*); the sense is: perform the preservation of that [knowledge] through non-forgetfulness and so on. These mantras are for the purpose of recitation (*japa*) by one desiring *medhā*. (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.4.1)

Now, the mantras for one desiring prosperity, which serve the purpose of the *homa* sacrifice, are being stated: "Bringing" (*āvahantī*) means leading near; "spreading" (*vitanvānā*) means extending, because the root *tan* has that as its object; "performing" (*kurvāṇā*) means accomplishing. "Without delay" (*acīram*) means not long, i.e., very quickly—the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic usage—or else it means "for a long time. What does he say? "Clothes" (*vāsāṃsi*), meaning garments, and "cows" (*gāvaḥ*), meaning cattle, for me—thus [he says]. "And" (*ca*) implies "and also. My own—what is that?—clothes and cows. That is the sense.

And whatever prosperity (*śrī*) one brings about by constantly providing food and drink and so forth—that prosperity, bring it from there after the production of intelligence (*medhā*). For the prosperity of one lacking intelligence leads only to misfortune. Of what kind? Bring it that which is "hairy" (*lomaśā*), meaning endowed with goats, sheep, and other such animals, as well as other livestock. By virtue of the context, it is the syllable *Oṃ* alone that is connected [to this]. *Svāhā*: the utterance *svāhā* is for the purpose of indicating the end of the mantra used for the oblation (*homa*). "May they come to me."

The phrase "may they come to me" is connected with what follows: "may the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*) come; may they measure out, may they understand, may they subdue, may they become tranquil," and so forth (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.4.2). "May I be glorious"—that is, may I be possessed of glory among the people, among the multitude of men. "May I be better"—meaning more praiseworthy than one who is "wealthier" (*vasyasaḥ*), that is, more wealthy (*vasīyasaḥ*) or more prosperous (*vasutarāt*); the meaning is: "may I be distinguished among those of my own kind, distinguished from a man of the same class who is merely wealthy."

Moreover, O Bhaga—O Blessed One, O Worshipful One—I shall enter you, who are the sheath of Brahman; and having entered, I shall become none other than your very self—this is the meaning. You too, O Bhaga—O Blessed One, O Worshipful One—enter me; let there be oneness between us alone. In you, who possess a thousand branches and many divisions, I wipe away my sinful deed. Just as in this world waters flow along a *pravat*—that is, along a downward slope, a low-lying place.

And just as the months are the "day-decayers" (*ahar-jaraḥ*) and the year is the "day-decayer"—meaning that by revolving through days it causes the worlds to decay, or else that the days decay within it and are contained therein—so too, O Ordainer (*dhātar*), O Creator of all, may the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*) come to me from all sides, from every direction. A "neighbor" (*prativeśaḥ*) is a place for removing fatigue, meaning a nearby house; such a neighbor art thou.

Like a neighbor, you are the place for those of virtuous conduct to remove all sins and sufferings; therefore, shine upon me, reveal yourself to me, and come to me—meaning, make me consist of you and have your own nature as your self, like iron permeated by mercury. In this section concerning knowledge (*vidyā*), "desire for prosperity" (*śrīkāma*) refers to the pursuit of wealth; wealth is for the sake of ritual action (*karman*); and ritual action is for the sake of destroying accumulated demerit (*durita*). For when that is destroyed, knowledge shines forth.
And so says the Smṛti: "Knowledge arises for men from the destruction of sinful karma; they behold the Self within themselves, as if in the surface of a clear mirror."
Thus ends the fourth section.

(TaittUBh 1.4.1–3) These three utterances (*vyāhṛti*) are indeed *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvaḥ*. Of these, Māhācamasya taught this fourth one: *mahaḥ*. That is Brahman; that is the Self (*ātman*); the other deities are its limbs. *Bhūḥ* is indeed this world; *bhuvaḥ* is the intermediate space; *suvaḥ* is yonder world. (TaittU 1.5.1)

*Mahas* is the sun; indeed, by the sun all the worlds are magnified (*mahīyante*). *Bhūḥ* is fire; *bhuvaḥ* is wind; *suvar* is the sun; *mahas* is the moon; indeed, by the moon all the luminaries are magnified. *Bhūḥ* is the *ṛc*s; *bhuvaḥ* is the *sāmans*; *suvar* is the *yajus*s.

"Mahas" is Brahman. Indeed, by means of Brahman all the Vedas are magnified. "Bhūḥ" is indeed the out-breath (prāṇa). "Bhuvaḥ" is the in-breath (apāna). "Suvaḥ" is the diffused breath (vyāna). "Mahas" is food. Indeed, by means of food all the vital breaths are magnified. These four [sets] are fourfold; there are four times four sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis). He who knows them knows Brahman. All the gods bring him tribute. Thus ends the fifth section. 5.

The meditation concerning the *saṃhitā* has been explained; following that, the mantras for one desiring intelligence and for one desiring prosperity have been set forth, and these too are intended solely for the application of knowledge through a traditional succession. Immediately thereafter, the meditation upon Brahman as consisting of the *vyāhṛtis*, which has self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) as its fruit, is introduced. "Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvar"—the word "iti" (thus) is for the purpose of indicating what has been stated, and "these three" is for the purpose of referring back to those already indicated. Those referred back are recalled by the phrase "verily, [they are] remembered."

This means that these three well-known *vyāhṛtis* are traditionally remembered; this fourth *vyāhṛti*, namely "Mahas," belongs to them. Māhācamasya—the offspring of Mahācamasa—proclaims this fourth one. The particle "u ha sma" is used for the purpose of relating a past event, meaning that he knew or perceived it. The mention of Māhācamasya is for the purpose of recollecting the seer (*ṛṣi*). It is understood from the instruction here that the recollection of the seer is also an auxiliary part of the meditation (*upāsanā*).

This *vyāhṛti* which is "Maha" according to Mahācamasya—that is Brahman, for Brahman is great (*mahat*) and the *vyāhṛti* is "Maha. But what is that? It is the Self (*ātman*). It is the Self because of the root *āp*, meaning "to pervade. And the other *vyāhṛtis*—the worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and the vital breaths—are pervaded by this *vyāhṛti*-Self, which exists as the sun, the moon, Brahman, and food. Therefore, the other deities are its limbs, its parts. The mention of "deities" is intended as an illustration for the worlds and the rest.

Since all things—the gods, the worlds, and so forth—are constituent parts of this *vyāhṛti* which is *mahat*, he says: "The worlds and so forth are magnified (*mahīyante*) by means of the sun and the rest. For the limbs of a self are magnified; "magnification" (*mahanam*) means growth or increase. Thus, "they are magnified" means they grow. This world, fire, the *Ṛgveda*, and the out-breath (*prāṇa*) constitute the first *vyāhṛti*, "bhūḥ. The intermediate space, the wind, the *Sāmaveda*, and the diffused breath (*apāna*) constitute the second *vyāhṛti*, "bhuvaḥ."

"That world" is the sun, "the sacrificial formulas" are the diffused breath (*vyāna*); this is the third *vyāhṛti*, "suvaḥ. "The sun" is the moon, "Brahman" is food; this is the fourth *vyāhṛti*, "mahaḥ. In this manner, each successive one becomes fourfold.

"Mahas" is Brahman; "Brahman" is the syllable *oṃ*, because in the context of sound, nothing else is possible. The rest has already been explained. "These indeed are four, and [each] fourth"—these indeed are the four: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *suvaḥ*, and *mahas*. Each one is fourfold, meaning they have four modes. The word *dhā* expresses the sense of mode. The meaning is that being four each, they become fourfold. The repetition of these as they were previously established is for the purpose of restricting their meditation exactly in that manner.

He who knows those aforementioned *vyāhṛtis* knows—that is, understands—that Brahman. What is that Brahman? [Objection: But surely, since it has been known that "that Brahman is the Self," one should not say "he knows Brahman" as if it were unknown. [Reply: No! There is no fault here, because the intention is to state its specific qualities. It is true that Brahman, the Self, has been known through the fourth *vyāhṛti*; however, its specific qualities—such as being perceivable within the heart, consisting of mind (*manomaya*), and so forth—have not yet been stated.

The group of attributes (*dharmapūga*) consisting of qualifications and qualified objects, ending with "abounding in peace" (*śāntisamṛddham*), is not understood [in its full extent]. Desiring to explain that, the author of the treatise, considering Brahman as if unknown, says, "He who knows Brahman. Therefore, there is no fault. The intention is: he who knows Brahman as distinguished by the group of attributes to be described hereafter, he knows Brahman. Consequently, this [verse] forms a single syntactical unit with the subsequent section (*anuvāka*), for the meditation (*upāsana*) is one and the same in both sections. This is also evident from internal indicative marks (*liṅga*).

The indicative mark (liṅga) beginning with "By *bhūḥ* he becomes established in Agni" points to the unity of the meditation; furthermore, there is an absence of an injunction [for separate meditations]. Indeed, there is no word that serves as an injunction such as "One should meditate on the Veda. And in the section on the *vyāhṛtis*, the phrase "he who knows this" does not differentiate the meditations, because its purpose will be stated later. That it has a purpose to be stated later is explained by the words "because of the desire to describe its specific details," and so forth. The meaning is: "All the gods bring (*āvahanti*)—that is, they lead (*ānayanti*)—the power (*bālīm*) to this very person who possesses such knowledge, once self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) has been attained."
Thus ends the fifth section.

(TaittUBh_1,5.1–3) It has been stated that the other deities are limbs of the Brahman whose nature consists of the vyāhṛtis *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, and *mahaḥ*. For the sake of the direct perception and the meditation upon this very Brahman of which they are the limbs, the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) is declared to be its locus, just as the *śālagrāma* stone is for Viṣṇu. For when that Brahman is meditated upon therein—distinguished by attributes such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*)—it is directly perceived, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand.
And since the path must be described for the sake of attaining every form of self-existence, this section is commenced:

"That which is this space within the heart—in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal, golden. Between the two palates is that which hangs down like a nipple; that is the source of Indra. Where the hair-parting turns, having pushed aside the two skull-halves, he stands firm in fire with the syllable *bhūḥ*, and in wind with *bhuvaḥ*. (TaittU 1.6.1)

The word "he" (saḥ), having been displaced, is connected with the phrase "this person" (ayaṃ puruṣaḥ). "Within the heart" means inside the heart. The "heart" is a lotus-shaped mass of flesh, the abode of the vital breaths (prāṇa), containing many tubular channels (nāḍīs), with its opening upward and its base downward; it is well-known and perceived when an animal is being dissected. Within that [heart] is this space (ākāśa), which is well-known just like the space within a water-pot (karakākāśa). In that [space] is this very person.

He is called *puruṣa* because he has filled (*pūrita*) the city (*puri*), or because he has filled the worlds beginning with the earth; he is "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*). "Mind" (*manas*) is consciousness (*vijñāna*). He is "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*) because he is perceived through it, as it is the instrument of the act of knowing (*manuti*). Or, "mind" is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) so called because one thinks (*manute*) by means of it; he is "consisting of that" because he identifies with it, or because it is his characteristic mark. He is "immortal" (*amṛta*), meaning his nature is not subject to death; he is "golden" (*hiraṇmaya*), meaning he consists of light (*jyotirmaya*).

The path for the realization of the nature of the Lord—which is of the same character as that which has been directly realized by the wise one in the space of the heart and has become his very self—is now described. The channel named Suṣumnā, well-known in the Yoga scriptures, proceeds upward from the heart; it goes between the two well-known palates in the middle. And "between" refers to the interior of that piece of flesh which hangs down like a breast in the middle of the two palates.

And where the "end of the hair"—the end, the limit, the root of the hairs—is "turned back," meaning it turns apart or diverges; having reached that region, [the path] has issued forth there. Having pushed aside, divided, and split open the two skull-halves (*śīrṣakapāle*), i.e., the cranial bones, it has emerged as that which is the "womb of Indra" (*sendrayoni*). The meaning is that it is the womb, the path, of Indra—that is, of Brahman—the gateway for attaining one's true nature.

Thus, one who knows this, perceiving the Self as consisting of mind, having departed through the crown of the head, becomes established in that fire which is the presiding deity of this world—the fire which is the form of the *vyāhṛti* "Bhūḥ" and is a limb of the Great Brahman; the meaning is that he pervades this world by means of the nature of fire. Likewise, he is established in the wind, which is the essence of the second *vyāhṛti*, "Bhuvaḥ"; the phrase "he is established" is understood to carry over.

"Suvaḥ" is in the sun; "Mahaḥ" is in Brahman. He attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*); he attains the Lord of the mind. He becomes the lord of speech, the lord of sight, the lord of hearing, and the lord of discernment. From that, he becomes this: Brahman whose body is space, whose self is truth, who delights in vital breath, whose joy is the mind, who is perfected in peace, and who is immortal. "Worship thus, O Prācīnayogya! Thus ends the sixth section.

In "Svaḥ," he is established in the Sun, which is the third *vyāhṛti* and his own self; in "Mahaḥ," he is established in Brahman, which is the whole and the fourth *vyāhṛti*. Having remained within these as their very essence, having become Brahman, he attains sovereignty—the state of being a self-ruler—and becomes himself a king and sovereign, just as Brahman is to the gods who constitute its limbs. And all the gods bring him tribute, just as they do to Brahman as their constituent part. He attains the Lord of the Mind (*manasaspati*).

For he is the lord of all minds because Brahman is the self of all; indeed, by means of all minds, he thinks that [Brahman]. Thus knowing, he attains it. Furthermore, he becomes the lord of all speech, the lord of all eyes, the lord of all ears, and the lord of all cognitions. Because he is the self of all, the meaning is that he comes to possess those [faculties] through the instruments of all living beings.

Moreover, this is even more than that. What is it? It is said: "having space for its body" (*ākāśaśarīra*). Its body is space, or its body is as subtle as space; thus it is "having space for its body. What is that? It is the Brahman under discussion. "Having truth for its self" (*satyātman*): truth is its form—whether manifest or unmanifest, non-false—or truth is its self-nature (*ātman*); thus it is "having truth for its self. "Delighting in the vital breaths" (*prāṇārāma*): that whose play and delight are among the vital breaths is "delighting in the vital breaths."

That in which the vital breaths (prāṇas) find their delight is "prāṇārāma. "Manasānanda" means that whose mind is blissful—that is, which produces happiness alone—is "manasānanda. "Śāntisamṛddha" means "śānti" is tranquility; that which is abundant in tranquility, or that which is attained through tranquility, is "śāntisamṛddha. "Amṛta" means having the nature of immortality. This further qualification is to be understood as applying specifically to the description beginning with "consisting of mind" (manomaya).
"O Prācīnayogya, meditate upon Brahman as described, distinguished by such qualities as consisting of mind and so forth"—this statement by the teacher is intended to show respect.
Thus ends the sixth section.

(TaittUBh 1.6.2) That Brahman consisting of the *vyāhṛtis* which was previously described as the object of meditation is now taught as an object of meditation in its form as the fivefold (*pāṅkta*) universe beginning with the earth. Because it possesses the number five, there is a correspondence with the *paṅkti* metre; consequently, everything is fivefold. And the sacrifice is fivefold, according to the Vedic revelation: "The *paṅkti* has five feet; the sacrifice is fivefold. Therefore, when one conceives of everything—from the worlds down to the self—as being fivefold, one conceives of it precisely as the sacrifice.
By means of that sacrifice thus conceived, one attains Prajāpati, who consists of the fivefold. To the question, "In what way is all this fivefold? he says:

The earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the quarters, and the intermediate quarters; fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars; water, herbs, trees, space, and the self—this is with respect to the elements (*adhibhūta*). Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the in-breath (*apāna*), the upward-breath (*udāna*), and the equalizing breath (*samāna*); the eye, the ear, the mind, speech, and the skin; the skin, flesh, sinews, bone, and marrow. Having analyzed this, the Seer said: "All this is indeed fivefold (*pāṅkta*); by means of the fivefold, one gains mastery over the fivefold. Thus ends the seventh section.

"Earth, intermediate space, heaven, the quarters, and the intermediate quarters" constitutes the pentad of worlds (*lokapañcaka*). "Fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars" constitutes the pentad of deities (*devatāpañcaka*). "Water, herbs, trees, space, and the self" constitutes the pentad of beings (*bhūtapañcaka*); here, "the self" refers to the *virāj*, because the context concerns beings. This [classification] pertains to the elemental realm (*adhibhūta*), and is intended to indicate the two pentads of worlds and deities, since both the pentads of worlds and deities have already been mentioned.

Immediately thereafter, the three pentads pertaining to the internal self (*adhyātma*) are described: the pentad of vital airs beginning with *prāṇa*; the pentad of sense organs beginning with the eye; and the pentad of elements beginning with the skin. For this much indeed constitutes everything that is internal. And the external is likewise a pentad. Having thus analyzed and conceived this, a seer (*ṛṣi*)—either one endowed with such vision or some other seer—spoke, that is, declared it.

Why is this so? It is said: "All this is fivefold (pāṅkta). By means of the fivefold internal [self], through the commonality of number, one strengthens, supports, and fulfills the fivefold external [world]. That is to say, it is perceived as having a single essence. Thus, the meaning is that he who knows "all this is fivefold" becomes the very self of Prajāpati. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.7.1)
Thus ends the seventh section.

"Om is Brahman. Om is all this. Indeed, they always respond with 'Om' when they say, 'Make him hear! They sing the *Sāmans* with 'Om'. They recite the *Śastras* with 'Oṃ Śom'. With 'Om', the Adhvaryu priest utters the response. With 'Om', the Brahman priest gives the impulse. With 'Om', one authorizes the Agnihotra sacrifice. When a Brāhmaṇa is about to speak, he says, 'May I attain Brahman'; he indeed attains Brahman. Thus ends the eighth section. 8.

The meditation upon the Self as Brahman has been described; immediately following that, the meditation upon that very same Self in the form of the fivefold sacrifice (*pāṅkta*) was described. Now, the meditation upon the syllable *Oṃ*, which serves as a limb for all meditations, is intended to be taught. For when the syllable *Oṃ* is meditated upon through the vision of the higher and lower Brahman, even as a mere sound, it becomes a means for attaining the higher and lower Brahman. Indeed, it is the support for both the higher and lower Brahman, just as an image is for Viṣṇu.

"By this very gateway one follows after either [of the two]," according to the Śruti. "Om. The word *iti* is for the purpose of delimiting the essential form. One should hold in the mind and meditate upon this syllable-form "Om" as Brahman; for everything here is of the nature of sound, and all is pervaded by the syllable Om. This is known from another Śruti passage: "As by a peg... Since the denoted is dependent upon the denoter, therefore all this is said to be the syllable Om. The subsequent text is for the purpose of praising the syllable Om.

Because that [Brahman] is to be meditated upon, "Om" is its imitation (anukṛti), that is, its imitation. When another person says, "I shall do it," or "I shall go," having performed or spoken, he imitates that by saying "Om. Therefore, the syllable Om is an imitation. The particles *ha*, *sma*, and *vai* indicate well-known facts; for the fact that the syllable Om is an imitation is indeed well known. Furthermore, preceded by the command "O, cause to hear! (*o śrāvaya*), they cause the announcement to be made and respond to it. Likewise, the chanters of the Sāmans sing the Sāmans with "Om"; and those who recite the Śastras also recite the Śastras with "Om śom."

"Thus," says the *adhvaryu*, as he utters the response (*pratigara*). "Om," says the *brahmā*, as he impels or gives permission. "Om," he says when giving permission for the *agnihotra*. When [the sacrificer] says, "I offer," he grants permission with "Om" alone. "Om," indeed, says a *brāhmaṇa* when about to speak—that is, when about to perform a recitation or being about to study; "Om," he says, meaning that he begins the study. Thinking, "May I attain the *brahman*—that is, the Veda"—he attains the *brahman*, thinking, "I shall grasp it. Thus he truly attains the *brahman*.

Alternatively, intending to declare or lead the Self forward with the thought, "May I attain Brahman, the Supreme Self," one says simply "Om. And by means of that syllable Om, one indeed attains Brahman. Since actions preceded by the syllable Om possess fruitfulness, the meaning of the sentence is: "Therefore, one should meditate upon the syllable Om as Brahman."
Thus ends the eighth section.

(Righteousness) and study and teaching of the Veda; truth and study and teaching of the Veda; austerity and study and teaching of the Veda; self-control and study and teaching of the Veda; tranquility and study and teaching of the Veda; the sacred fires and study and teaching of the Veda; the fire-sacrifice and study and teaching of the Veda; guests and study and teaching of the Veda; human duties and study and teaching of the Veda; and progeny and study and teaching of the Veda.

"Offspring and the study and teaching of the Veda," says Satyavacas Rāthītara. "Offspring and the study and teaching of the Veda," says Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi. "Only the study and teaching of the Veda," says Nāka Maudgalya; for that indeed is austerity, that indeed is austerity.
Thus ends the ninth Anuvāka.

Since it has been stated that "one attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) from consciousness alone," it might follow that the rituals prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* are useless. To prevent this conclusion, these [rituals] are introduced here in order to demonstrate that they are means toward the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). "Truth" (*ṛta*) has already been explained. "Self-study" (*svādhyāya*) is the act of studying; "expounding" (*pravacana*) is teaching or the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The completion of the sentence is: "These, beginning with truth, are to be performed."

Truth is truthful speech, or austerity (*tapas*) as previously explained, such as the *kṛcchra* penance and others. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the calming of the external organs; tranquility (*śama*) is the calming of the internal organ. The sacred fires are to be established; the *agnihotra* sacrifice is to be offered; and guests are to be honored. "Human" refers to worldly social conduct, and that should be performed according to what has been traditionally received. Offspring are to be produced; "procreation" (*prajana*) means approaching one's wife during her fertile season.

“Procreation” means the birth of a grandson, [implying] that a son must be established in a household. Although one may be engaged in all these duties, the study and teaching of the Veda (*svādhyāya-pravacana*) must be performed with diligent effort; for this purpose, the mention of “study and teaching” is made alongside every other duty. For the knowledge of the meaning depends upon the study of the Veda, and the highest good depends upon the knowledge of the meaning. Furthermore, teaching is for the sake of not forgetting it and for the increase of Dharma.

Therefore, one should apply oneself with diligence to the study and recitation of the Vedas. *Satyavacas*: he whose speech is indeed truth; this is his name, or it may be his name. *Rāthītara*: the teacher Rāthītara, belonging to the Rathītara lineage, holds this view. *Taponitya*: "Austerity alone must be practiced"; he is constant in austerity, devoted to austerity, or alternatively, he is named Taponitya.

Pauruśiṣṭi, the descendant of Puruśiṣṭa, the teacher, maintains that only the private study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) and its exposition (*pravacana*) are to be practiced. Nāka by name, the son of Mudgala—the Maudgalya teacher—maintains the same. "For that indeed is austerity, for that indeed is austerity. Because *svādhyāya* and *pravacana* alone constitute austerity, therefore those two alone are to be practiced. Although truthfulness, austerity, *svādhyāya*, and exposition have already been mentioned, they are mentioned again for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the ninth section.

(I am) the shaker of the tree; my fame is like the back of a mountain. With my purifier raised up, like a prize-winning steed, I am my own nectar—wealthful and resplendent. O wise one, I am sprinkled with immortality. Thus ends the Vedic recitation of Triśaṅku. This is the tenth section. 10.

The traditional recitation of the mantra, "I am the impeller of the tree," is for the purpose of private study (*svādhyāya*), and private study leads to the arising of knowledge, according to the context; for this entire section has knowledge as its purpose, and no other purpose is perceived. Furthermore, the arising of knowledge is possible for one whose being (*sattva*) has been purified by private study. [The meaning is: "I am the impeller (*rerivā*), the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), of the tree—of the tree of *saṃsāra* which is characterized by destruction. My fame (*kīrtiḥ*), my renown (*khyātiḥ*), is as elevated as the peak of a mountain."

"Ūrdhvapavitra" means that for me, the Self of all, the supreme Brahman—which is the upward-purifying, the upward-cause, the purifier, and that which is revealed by knowledge—is the "ūrdhvapavitra. "Vājinīva" means like Savitṛ who possesses "vāja," that is, food; the meaning is "like Savitṛ. Just as the immortal reality of the Self (ātmatattva), which is pure and well-known from hundreds of Śruti and Smṛti texts, is established in Savitṛ, even so am I my own immortal, beautiful, and pure reality of the Self. I exist as such.

"Draviṇam" means wealth; "savarcasam" means radiant or luminous. That very thing follows [the thought], "I am that reality of the Self. Alternatively, the knowledge of Brahman is "savarcasam" because it illuminates the reality of the Self. It is called "draviṇam" (wealth) because, like wealth, it is the cause of the bliss of liberation. In this interpretation, the word "mayā" (by me) must be supplied [to complete the sense]. "Sumedhāḥ": I am one whose intelligence (*medhā*) is excellent (*su*), characterized by omniscience; thus I am "sumedhāḥ. One is "sumedhāḥ" through the possession of skill (*kauśalya*) in the maintenance, origination, and dissolution of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Therefore, he is "immortal" (*amṛta*), meaning one whose nature is not subject to death, who is undecaying (*akṣita*), inexhaustible (*avyaya*), or one who has been sprinkled (*ukṣita*) with the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). The Brāhmaṇa passage says, "I have been sprinkled with the nectar of immortality," and so forth. Thus, this is the "recitation of the Veda" (*vedānuvacana*) of the seer Triśaṅku, who had become Brahman and was a knower of Brahman. Here, "Veda" means the knowledge of the oneness of the Self; "recitation of the Veda" refers to the verbal expression following upon the attainment of that [knowledge].

The meaning is that, like Vāmadeva, for the sake of proclaiming his own fulfillment of all duties, Triśaṅku perceived through seer-vision (*ārṣa-darśana*) the collection of mantras which reveals the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). It is understood that the recitation (*japa*) of this [text] is for the purpose of generating that knowledge; this is understood from the subsequent mention of duties beginning with "Truth" (*ṛtam*) and the recitation of the Vedic study (*vedānuvacana*).

Thus, for one who is engaged in the obligatory rites of the Śruti and Smṛti, who is free from desire, and who seeks to know the Supreme Brahman, there arise seer-visions concerning the Self and other such subjects.
Thus ends the tenth Anuvāka.

(TaittUBh_1,10.1) Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: "Speak the truth. Practice righteousness. Do not neglect your private Vedic study. Having brought wealth that is pleasing to your teacher, do not let the lineage of progeny be cut off. One must not swerve from the truth. One must not swerve from righteousness. One must not swerve from what is beneficial. One must not swerve from prosperity. One must not swerve from private Vedic study and its recitation. (TaittU_1,11.1)

One must not neglect the rites for the gods and the ancestors. Be one who regards the mother as a god; be one who regards the father as a god; be one who regards the teacher as a god; be one who regards the guest as a god. Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, and not others. Those well-performed deeds of ours should be emulated by you.

Not others. Whatever Brahmins there may be who are more excellent and better than you, you should breathe out [your fatigue] by offering them a seat. One should give with faith; one should not give without faith. One should give with dignity; one should give with modesty; one should give with fear; one should give with a sense of social obligation. Now, if you should have any doubt regarding ritual action or any doubt regarding conduct—

In that regard, you should conduct yourself among those Brahmins who are reflective, disciplined, diligent, free from harshness, and lovers of dharma—just as they conduct themselves there. And likewise among those who have been accused: you should conduct yourself among those Brahmins who are reflective, disciplined, diligent, free from harshness, and lovers of dharma—just as they conduct themselves toward them. This is the instruction; this is the teaching; this is the secret doctrine of the Veda (*vedopaniṣad*); this is the precept. Thus it should be honored; thus indeed should it be honored.
Thus ends the eleventh section. 11.

The commencement of the instruction on duties, beginning with "having studied the Veda," has the following meaning: prior to the realization of Brahman, the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis must be performed as a rule. This is because the scriptural injunction regarding instruction (anuśāsana) is for the purpose of purifying the person; for in one whose being is purified through such refinement, knowledge of the Self arises easily. As the Smṛti says: "By austerity one destroys impurity; by knowledge one attains immortality. And the text will later state: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity."

Therefore, rituals are to be performed for the sake of the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*). This is because of the word "instruction" (*anuśāsana*) in the phrase "he instructs," for indeed, a fault arises from the transgression of instruction. Furthermore, because of their prior mention—since rituals were introduced before the commencement of the exclusive knowledge of Brahman—and because once the knowledge of Brahman has arisen, [the text] will demonstrate the uselessness of rituals through such passages as, "He finds fearless support; he fears nothing at all; 'Why have I not done what is good? and so forth.

Therefore, it is understood that ritual actions serve as means for the arising of knowledge by way of destroying previously accumulated demerits. This is also evident from the wording of the mantra: "Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge. The instruction regarding the *ṛta* and other duties in the previous section was intended to avoid their becoming purposeless; here, however, since they serve the purpose of generating knowledge, they are intended to establish a rule of what must be performed.

Having taught and instructed the Veda to his resident pupil (antevāsī), the teacher instructs him; that is to say, he instructs him subsequently to the mastery of the text, meaning he causes him to grasp its meaning. From this it is understood that one who has studied the Veda must not return from the teacher’s house without having undertaken the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*). This is also supported by the Smṛti: "And having understood [the Veda], one should begin the ritual acts. How does he instruct? He says: "Speak the truth"—that which ought to be spoken as it is known through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—and likewise, "practice Dharma."

"Dharma" is a general term for those things that ought to be performed, since specific qualifications such as "truth" and so forth are subsequently specified. Do not be negligent—that is, do not commit negligence—regarding *svādhyāya*, which is Vedic study. Having brought and given to the teacher wealth that is dear and desired for the sake of the teacher, in order to pay for his knowledge, and having been permitted by the teacher, one should take a suitable wife and not cut off the thread of progeny; the lineage of progeny must not be severed.

The intention is that even though a son has not yet been born, one must exert effort toward his birth through such actions as the desire for a son; this is because of the force of the instruction regarding the triad of *prajā*, *prajanana*, and *prajāti*. Otherwise, he would have mentioned only "procreation" (*prajanana*). One must not be negligent regarding truth; negligence must not be practiced. And negligence regarding truth is the occurrence of falsehood, by the force of the word "negligence. The meaning is that one must not speak untruth even through forgetfulness.

Otherwise, there would be merely a prohibition against speaking untruths. Regarding the injunction "one must not be negligent (*pramaditavyam*) with respect to *dharma*": since the word *dharma* refers to that which is to be practiced, negligence consists in non-performance; that [negligence] must not be committed, meaning that *dharma* must indeed be performed. Likewise, one must not be negligent regarding wholesome actions that serve to protect oneself. *Bhūti* means prosperity; for the sake of that prosperity (*bhūtyai*), one must not be negligent regarding auspicious actions conducive to prosperity.

"One should not neglect the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) and its proclamation (*pravacana*). *Svādhyāya* means study; *pravacana* means teaching. The meaning is that one must perform these two as a matter of rule. Likewise, "one should not neglect the rites for the gods and the ancestors (*devapitṛkārya*)," meaning the rituals for the gods and the ancestors must be performed. "Be one for whom the mother is a god (*mātṛdeva*)," that is, you should become such a person. In the same way, "be one for whom the father is a god," "be one for whom the teacher is a god," and "be one for whom the guest is a god."

The meaning is that these [practices] are to be venerated like deities. Furthermore, whatever other blameless and irreproachable actions are characterized by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), those should be practiced and performed by you; others, even if performed by the learned, which are blameworthy, must not be done. Those very good deeds—the beautiful conducts of us, your teachers—which are not in contradiction with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) and so forth, are to be venerated by you; they are to be carried out for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), meaning they must be performed as a matter of rule.

Not others who act contrarily, even if they have been made teachers. And whoever are distinguished by qualities such as being teachers and so forth, who are superior to us and more praiseworthy than we—those are Brāhmaṇas, not Kṣatriyas and the like. By means of their seat—that is, by the offering of a seat and so forth—you must relieve their fatigue. "Praśvasana" (relieving) is "praśvāsa" (relief); the meaning is that you must remove their weariness.

When their assembly has gathered for the purpose of a social gathering, one should not sigh among them, nor should even a sigh be made; rather, one should simply grasp the essence of what they have said. Furthermore, whatever is to be given must be given with faith alone; that which is not to be given should not be given without faith. That which is to be given should be given with prosperity and abundance, with modesty and shame, with fear and dread, and with mindfulness—mindfulness being the performance of duties such as those concerning mantras and the like.

Now, if while you are conducting yourself in this manner, at any time a doubt or uncertainty should arise regarding a ritual act prescribed by the Śruti or Smṛti, or regarding conduct characterized by proper behavior—then, in that place or at that time, those Brāhmaṇas who are engaged in such rituals and conduct must be understood (through the ellipsis) as being "deliberate," meaning capable of reflection; "engaged," meaning devoted to ritual or conduct; "unemployed," meaning not employed by others; and "gentle," meaning not harsh, possessing minds free from cruelty.

"Those who desire dharma, who seek the unseen goal, and who are not overcome by desire"—these would be, they should be, such persons. Those brahmins, in whatever manner and by whatever means they might conduct themselves in that action or in their livelihood, in that same way you too should conduct yourself. Furthermore, regarding those who have been falsely accused—those who have been charged with a fault by someone through a doubtful charge—in their case as well, one should apply everything as previously stated, beginning with "those who are there," and so forth. This is the instruction; this is the rule.

This is the instruction for fathers and others toward their sons and others. This is the secret of the Veda (*vedopaniṣad*), the mystery of the Veda, and the meaning of the Veda; this alone is the teaching (*anuśāsana*), the word of the Lord, because it has been stated as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) in the form of an authoritative statement. Or rather, this is the instruction of all that constitutes valid authority (*pramāṇa*). Since it is so, therefore everything as described must be meditated upon and performed.
The repetition—"this indeed is to be meditated upon, this indeed is to be meditated upon, and not not to be meditated upon"—is for the sake of showing reverence. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.4)

In this regard, the following is considered for the sake of distinguishing between knowledge (*vidyā*) and action (*karman*): Is the supreme good attained from actions alone; or from actions accompanied by knowledge; or from knowledge and action combined; or from knowledge that requires action; or indeed from knowledge alone? On this point, it might be argued that it is from actions alone, because one who possesses knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda is entitled to perform ritual action.

For there is a traditional injunction (smṛti) stating: "The entire Veda, together with its secret portions (rahasya), must be mastered by the twice-born. And "mastering" includes the meaning of the Upaniṣads, such as the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) and so forth. Furthermore, in every instance, it is shown that only the learned man has the qualification for ritual action, as in the statements: "The learned man sacrifices" and "The learned man officiates at a sacrifice. Also, there is the principle: "Performance [of rites] follows from knowing [the texts]. Moreover, some maintain that the entire Veda is for the purpose of ritual action; for if the supreme good were not attained through rituals, the Veda would be useless. This is not so.

Because liberation is eternal; for liberation is held to be eternal. It is well known in the world that the product of action is non-eternal, and if the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) resulting from actions were non-eternal, that would be undesirable. If it is argued that liberation does not depend on knowledge because—due to the non-commencement of optional and prohibited rites, the exhaustion through experience alone of commenced karma, and the impossibility of transgression due to the performance of obligatory duties—liberation is attained independently of knowledge, that too is not so.

It has already been refuted that the production of another body caused by that [residual karma] would follow because of the possibility of residual karma (*śeṣakarman*), and also that the exhaustion of residual karma is impossible because it is not contradicted by the performance of obligatory duties (*nitya*). Furthermore, as for what was said—that one who possesses knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda is qualified for ritual action (*karman*) and so forth—that is also not the case; for meditation (*upāsanā*) is distinct from the knowledge derived from hearing (*śrutajñāna*). Indeed, one is qualified for ritual action through the mere knowledge derived from hearing, and does not depend upon meditation.

Furthermore, meditation (*upāsana*) is enjoined as something distinct from the knowledge derived from hearing (*śruta-jñāna*), having liberation as its fruit; and this would follow because it is established as a distinct entity. Having stated that "it is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*), there is the injunction of other efforts in the form of "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*) and "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*); thus, reflection and meditation are well-known to be distinct from the knowledge gained through hearing. If this is so, then liberation would result from ritual actions that depend upon such knowledge.

If it is argued that actions accompanied by knowledge possess the capacity to initiate a different effect—just as poisons, curd, and the like, though naturally capable of initiating effects such as death or fever, acquire the capacity to initiate a different effect when combined with mantras, sugar, and so forth; and likewise, if it is claimed that liberation is initiated by actions accompanied by knowledge—we say: no. For the fault has already been stated: that which is produced (ārabhya) is non-eternal. If it is argued that it is indeed eternal even though produced because of a scriptural statement, we say: no, because a scriptural statement serves only to make known (jñāpaka) what already exists.

A statement is a communicator of a thing as it truly is, not the creator of something non-existent. For even by means of a hundred statements, that which is eternal cannot be begun, nor can that which has been begun become indestructible. By this, the claim that knowledge (*vidyā*) and action (*karman*), when combined, initiate liberation (*mokṣa*) is refuted. If it is argued that knowledge and action merely remove the causes that obstruct liberation, we say no; for action is observed to have other fruits. Indeed, the fruits of action are seen to be origination, refinement, transformation, and attainment.

Furthermore, liberation is the opposite of results such as birth and so forth. If it is argued that liberation is something to be attained because of scriptural texts concerning "going"—that is, because of such scriptural passages on going as "moving upwards by way of the door of the sun" and so on—we say no. This is because Brahman is omnipresent and because it is non-different from those who go. Since Brahman is the cause of ether and the rest, it is omnipresent; and all individual conscious selves (*vijñānātman*) are non-distinct from Brahman. Therefore, liberation is not something to be attained. For that which is to be reached by a traveler must be a different location distinct from the traveler.

For that which is non-different from something cannot be understood by that very same thing; and the establishment of this non-difference is known from hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts such as, "Having created that, He entered into it," and "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field. If it is argued that there is a contradiction with scriptural passages concerning movement and sovereignty, [the response is: even so, if liberation were unattainable, then...

If it is argued that there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the paths of the departed, such as "He becomes one-fold," and with the scriptural texts regarding the desire for the world of the fathers, such as "or with women, or with vehicles," and so forth—[we reply: no, because those [texts] have the effected Brahman (kārya-brahman) as their object. For women and the like can exist in the effected Brahman, but not in the causal [Brahman], according to such scriptural passages as "One alone, without a second; where one sees nothing else, what could he see, and by what? Furthermore, due to this contradiction, the combination of knowledge and ritual action is untenable.

For knowledge, which has as its object the reality in which specific factors such as the agent and so forth have dissolved, is in contradiction with ritual action, which is to be accomplished by those very factors that are the opposite of such knowledge. Indeed, it is impossible for a single entity to be seen in two ways—as possessing specific distinctions such as agency from the perspective of ultimate reality, and yet as being devoid of them.

For one of the two must necessarily be false; and since the falsity of one follows, it is logical that duality—the object of innate ignorance—is false. This is established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "Where there is, as it were, duality, one goes from death to death"; "But where one sees another... that is the small"; and "He thinks, 'This one is other than I, and I am other than he,' and makes a separation within himself; then fear comes upon him. Thus it is known from these and other such texts.

And the truth of oneness is to be perceived in a single way through such scriptural passages as, "One should see [it] as one indeed," "Brahman alone is this all, without a second," and "The Self alone is this all. Furthermore, no ritual action is possible when there is no perception of the distinctions between the recipient of the gift and other factors of action (*kāraka*). Moreover, thousands of prohibitions against perceiving difference are heard in the context of knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, there is a contradiction between knowledge and ritual action; consequently, their combination (*samuccaya*) is untenable.

In this regard, that which was stated—that liberation results from knowledge and action combined—is untenable, because actions are enjoined. If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the Śruti: if the realization of the oneness of the Self is enjoined by subverting specific causal factors such as the agent and so forth—just like the cognition of a rope-substrate subverts the erroneous cognition of a snake and the like—then it follows that the scriptural injunctions regarding action would be rendered devoid of an object, resulting in contradiction. Yet, actions have indeed been enjoined; therefore, such a contradiction is not tenable.

If it is argued that [the scriptures] are authoritative because they are the Vedas, we say no; for the Vedas have as their primary purpose the instruction regarding the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). To begin with, the Veda is intent on teaching knowledge (*vidyā*) in the sense that "man must be liberated from saṃsāra," and thus it proceeds by illuminating knowledge so that the cessation of ignorance—the cause of saṃsāra—may be effected. Therefore, there is no contradiction. If it is further argued that even so, the scripture which teaches the existence of causal factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth remains contradictory, we say no.

The scripture, employing the existence of the causal factors (*kāraka*) exactly as they are perceived, prescribes ritual actions for the purpose of destroying accumulated demerit for those seeking liberation, and serves as a means to achieve results for those desiring fruits; it does not, however, concern itself with the ontological reality of the causal factors. For the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is not possible for one whose progress is obstructed by accumulated demerit. When that [demerit] is destroyed, knowledge arises; from that follows the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), and from that, the absolute end of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, for one who perceives no self, desire has the non-self as its object.

One who desires performs actions; from that arises *saṃsāra*, characterized by the appropriation of a body and so forth, for the sake of experiencing those results. Conversely, for one who perceives the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*), desire is impossible because, in the absence of objects, there is no basis for desire. Since desire is impossible when the Self is not distinct [from the objects], and since liberation (*mokṣa*) consists in abiding in one's own Self, knowledge and action are therefore in opposition. Precisely because of this opposition, knowledge does not depend upon actions with respect to liberation.

However, with respect to the attainment of one's own Self, obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) serve as causes for knowledge by means of removing the obstructions of previously accumulated sins; this is why we stated that the rites are introduced in this section. In this way, there is no contradiction with the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual action. Therefore, it is established that supreme bliss results from knowledge alone.

If that were so, then the existence of other stages of life (*āśrama*) would be untenable, because the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is caused by ritual action (*karman*), and such actions are prescribed specifically for the householder stage; thus, there would be only a single stage of life. Consequently, scriptural injunctions such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvaj-jīva*) would be more consistent [with this view]. [Reply: No, because actions are manifold. For ritual actions do not consist solely of the *agnihotra* and the like.

Furthermore, there exist such actions as celibacy, austerity, truthfulness, tranquility, self-restraint, non-violence, and so forth, which are well-known in the later stages of life (āśramas) and are unmixed [with worldly motives], serving as the most effective means for the arising of knowledge; these include characteristics such as meditation and concentration. And the author will state: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity."

Furthermore, since the arising of knowledge is possible even prior to entering the householder stage due to actions performed in previous lives, and since the adoption of the householder stage is for the sake of ritual action, once knowledge—which is to be accomplished through action—is already attained, the adoption of the householder stage would indeed be purposeless; this is also because sons and other such things exist for the sake of the world.

Furthermore, for one whose desires have turned away from these worldly ends—namely, the worlds to be accomplished through sons and so forth, as well as the world of the fathers and the world of the gods—and who perceives the eternally established Self, seeing no purpose in ritual action, how could engagement in action be possible? Even for one who has entered the householder stage, once knowledge has arisen and he becomes dispassionate through the maturation of that knowledge, seeing no purpose in rituals, there would necessarily be a cessation from actions.

If it is argued that [the renunciation of action] is improper because of the observation of scriptural indications such as "O, I am about to go forth from this state," and because one observes a greater effort toward ritual action in scripture—[we reply: there is indeed greater effort toward rituals such as the Agnihotra, and the exertion in ritual action is great because the Agnihotra and other rites must be accomplished through numerous means.

If it is argued that an equal option between [the householder's life] and the other stages of life is not appropriate for the householder—since austerity (*tapas*) and such practices, as well as the duties of the other stages, are equally present even in the householder stage, and since the others require fewer means (*alpasādhanāpekṣatva*)—we say no. This is because of the assistance provided by actions performed in previous births. As it was stated, "There is greater effort required for ritual action according to the Veda," and so forth; this is not a fault.

For actions performed in previous births—characterized by rites such as the *agnihotra* or by qualities such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*)—become supportive for the arising of knowledge. This is evidenced by the fact that some are seen to be dispassionate from birth itself, while others are engaged in ritual acts, lacking dispassion and even hostile toward knowledge. Therefore, it is accepted that those who possess the impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed in previous births and are dispassionate should indeed enter another stage of life (*āśrama*), especially because of the abundance of fruits resulting from ritual action.

Because the fruits of action—characterized by such things as sons, heaven, and spiritual luster—are innumerable, and because men have many desires regarding them, it is appropriate that the Śruti exerts greater effort toward those [fruits] in the context of ritual actions. This is evident from the abundance of prayers seen in the form, "May this be mine; may that be mine. Furthermore, it is because they are means; for we have already stated that ritual actions serve as the means to knowledge (*vidyā*). Greater effort must be applied toward the means, not toward the end.

If it is argued that because knowledge (*vidyā*) has action as its cause, other efforts are useless—namely, that if knowledge arises from actions alone through the destruction of the obstructions consisting of previously accumulated demerits (*durita*), then the effort of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, which is taught separately from actions in the *Upaniṣads*, is purposeless—we say no. This is because there is no such restrictive rule (*niyama*). For there is no fixed rule that knowledge arises only from the destruction of obstructions, and not rather from the grace of the Lord (*īśvara*), the performance of austerity (*tapas*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth.

Furthermore, since non-violence, celibacy, and so forth are supportive of knowledge, and since hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana) are its direct causes, the other stages of life (āśramas) are established as valid. Thus it is proven that all persons are entitled to the pursuit of knowledge, and that the supreme good consists solely in knowledge itself.

May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Homage to Brahman! Homage to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. To you alone, the perceptible Brahman, have I spoken. I have spoken the *ṛta*; I have spoken the truth. May that protect me; may that protect the speaker. It has protected me; it has protected the speaker. *Oṃ*. Peace, peace, peace. Thus ends the twelfth section.

For the purpose of pacifying the obstacles encountered in attaining past knowledge, he recites the *śānti* [verse] beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us. This has been explained previously. Thus ends the Chapter on Training (*śikṣādhyāya*).

May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu, the wide-strider, be auspicious to us. Homage to Brahman! Homage to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace!
Thus ends the twelfth section. 12.

The Brahmānanda Vallī. Om. May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us. May Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Salutations to Brahman! Salutations to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Satya. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker.
