May it protect me; may it protect the speaker. Om! May it protect us both together; may it nourish us both together.

"Let us two perform [this] with vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we not hate each other. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace! The *śānti* (propitiatory rite) beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" was recited previously for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the attainment of the knowledge already passed. Now, however, the *śānti* beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" and "May He protect us together" is recited for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to the attainment of the Brahma-knowledge that is about to be taught. The passage beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" is clear, as explained before.

May He protect us both—both the disciple and the teacher—together; may He protect us together. May He nourish us both with the knowledge of Brahman. May we together perform our work—that is, may we accomplish our capacity for the sake of knowledge and the like. May what we have studied be luminous for us both, for us who are luminous; that is to say, may it be fit for the understanding of its meaning.

"May we not hate each other. Since enmity might arise between the disciple and the teacher due to negligence regarding the acquisition of knowledge through some injustice, this benediction—"may we not hate each other"—is intended to pacify that. "May we not fall into mutual hatred. The threefold repetition of "Peace! Peace! Peace! has already been explained. Furthermore, this *śānti* (peace) is for the purpose of quelling obstacles to the knowledge about to be taught. The attainment of the science of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) is desired without hindrance, for that is the root of the supreme good (*paraṃ śreyaḥ*).

*Oṃ*. "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Regarding this, there is this verse: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. He who knows it as hidden in the secret cave of the heart, in the highest heaven—he, together with the wise Brahman, attains all desires. From that very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; and from food, the person (*puruṣa*).

This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food. Of him, this is the head; this is the right wing; this is the left wing; this is the trunk; this is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse:
(TaittU 2.1.1). Thus ends the first section. 1.

Meditations concerning the *saṃhitā* and other such topics, which are not in conflict with ritual actions (*karma*), have been described. Immediately following that, the vision of the Self as possessing internal limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) was taught by means of the *vyāhṛtis*, with sovereignty (*svārājya*) as its fruit. However, since the seed of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is not entirely eradicated by this much alone, this section beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" is commenced for the purpose of removing ignorance—the seed of all afflictions—and for the sake of the vision of the Self in which all specific limiting adjuncts have been shaken off.

The purpose of this knowledge of Brahman is the cessation of ignorance, and from that follows the absolute absence of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). As it will be said: "The knower does not fear anything from any quarter. For as long as the cause of *saṃsāra* exists, it would be impossible [to say] that "one finds fearless support" or that "what has been done and what has not been done—sin and merit—do not afflict one. Therefore, it is understood that from this realization, which has as its object Brahman as the Self of all, follows the absolute absence of *saṃsāra*.

And he himself states the purpose at the very beginning, in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," for the sake of making known the relationship and the purpose. For once the relationship and the purpose are fully understood, one proceeds toward the hearing, grasping, retaining, and repeated practice of this knowledge. Indeed, the fruit of knowledge is preceded by hearing and so forth, as established by other scriptural passages such as, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon."

The "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*) is one who knows—that is, fully realizes—Brahman, which will be defined by its characteristics later; it is called *brahman* because of its supreme greatness (*bṛhattama*). Such a knower attains the Supreme, the unsurpassed; that very Brahman is the Supreme. For there can be no attainment of one thing through the knowledge of another. Furthermore, another scriptural passage clearly shows that the attainment of Brahman belongs only to the knower of Brahman: "He who indeed knows that Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and so forth.

But will not the scripture declare that Brahman is omnipresent and the very self of all? Therefore, it cannot be attained; for attainment is observed to occur between one delimited thing and another delimited thing. Since Brahman is undivided and the self of all, its attainment—as if it were delimited and as if it were a non-self—is logically untenable. This is not a fault. Why? Because the attainment or non-attainment of Brahman depends upon perception and non-perception.

From the perspective of ultimate reality, although this individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of Brahman, it perceives itself as having the nature of the sheaths beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya), which are external limitations created by the subtle elements (bhūtamātra), and its mind is attached thereto.

Just as one who completes a given number fails to perceive his own true nature because his mind is distracted by external objects to be counted—despite being immediately present—so too, through ignorance characterized by the failure to perceive the nature of the supreme Brahman, one identifies the external non-selves, such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*), as the Self; thus, one conceives "I am not other than these non-selves like the *annamaya*. In this way, even though Brahman is one's very own self, it remains unattained due to ignorance.

Just as for that very Self—which, though its true nature as Brahman has not been attained due to ignorance, and which serves to complete the aforementioned number—there is a subsequent attainment of that same [nature] through knowledge once it has been reminded by someone; even so, the attainment of Brahman, who is taught in the Śruti as the Self of all, is indeed logically established through the knowledge consisting in the vision of His being one's own Self. The statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," is like a sūtra for the entire meaning of this section (vallī).

By the statement "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," Brahman is introduced as the object of knowledge; since its specific nature has not yet been determined, there follows a definition capable of imparting its specific nature as distinguished from all else, for the purpose of determining that nature. Furthermore, so that this Brahman—of which the knowledge was mentioned generally and whose definition will be stated later—may be specifically known as the inner self (*pratyagātman*) in a non-dual form, [the text proceeds]; and also regarding the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman which belongs to the knower of Brahman...

The characteristic of attaining the Supreme Brahman has been stated; however, this verse is cited in order to demonstrate that this state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*) is nothing other than the very nature of Brahman, which transcends all attributes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Thus it is said: "In this regard, this verse is recited. That is to say, with reference to the very subject matter expressed in the Brāhmaṇa passage, this verse is recited and handed down. The sentence "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" is intended to provide the definition of Brahman.

For the three words beginning with "truth" (*satya*) are qualifiers of the qualificand, Brahman. Brahman is the qualificand because it is intended to be known as the object of cognition. Since Brahman is intended primarily as that which is to be known, it must be understood as the qualificand. Therefore, precisely because of this relationship between qualifier and qualificand, the words beginning with "truth," ending in the same case-ending, are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Brahman, being qualified by the three qualifiers beginning with "truth," is distinguished from other things that are to be qualified; for it is only when something is distinguished from others that it becomes known, just as in the world one says, "a blue, large, fragrant lotus."

[Objection: Is it not the case that a qualificand is qualified by another qualifier when it deviates from it, as in "the blue and the red lotus"? For when there are multiple substances of the same genus possessing multiple qualifiers, then the qualifier has meaning. Indeed, in the case of a single entity—just as one says "this is the one sun"—another qualifier cannot apply; likewise, Brahman is one alone, and there are no other Brahmans by which it might be qualified as a blue lotus is. [Reply: No.

Because qualifiers have the purpose of defining, this fault does not apply. Why? Because qualifiers are primarily intended for the purpose of definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and not primarily for the sake of the qualifier itself. What, then, is the distinction between a definition and that which is defined, or between a qualifier and that which is qualified? It is said: qualifiers exclude the qualified only from things of the same class, whereas a definition excludes it from everything; for example, "space is that which provides room. And we have already stated that a sentence has the purpose of providing a definition.

The words "truth" and so forth are not mutually connected, because they are for the sake of another; for they have as their referent the substantive (the qualified object). Therefore, each individual qualifying term, being independent of the others, is connected with the word "Brahman"—namely: "Brahman is truth," "Brahman is knowledge," and "Brahman is infinite. That which, having been determined by a certain form, does not deviate from that form, is "truth. That which, having been determined by a certain form, deviates from that form, is called "untruth" (*anṛta*).

Therefore, the modification is immortal, yet the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; "clay alone is real"—because of this restriction that "only Being is real," Brahman is established as the Truth. Thus, by the phrase "Brahman is Truth," Brahman is distinguished from its modifications. Consequently, the status of being a cause accrues to Brahman. And for a cause, the state of being an agent follows, and because it is a real entity, the state of being insentient, like clay, would also follow; therefore, it is said: "Brahman is Knowledge."

Knowledge (*jñāna*) means cognition or understanding; the word *jñāna* here functions as a noun denoting the state itself (*bhāva-sādhana*), and not as the agent of knowing, because it qualifies Brahman along with "truth" (*satya*) and "infinitude" (*ananta*). Indeed, truth and infinitude are not possible if [Brahman] were the agent of knowing. For how could that which undergoes modification through being the agent of knowing be true and infinite? That which is not divided from anything whatsoever is infinite. If there were agency of knowing, [Brahman] would be divided by the object of knowledge and the act of knowing, and thus its infinitude would not exist.

According to another scriptural passage, "That wherein one knows nothing else is the Infinite (bhūman); but that wherein one knows something else is the finite. If it is argued that the phrase "one knows nothing else" implies a specific negation and thus means "one knows the Self," we say no; for the sentence is intended to enjoin the definition of the Infinite. The statement beginning with "wherein one sees nothing else" is a sentence intended to enjoin the defining characteristics of the Infinite.

Based on the well-known fact that one perceives another, the nature of the "Bhūman" (the Infinite) is made known there where that [perception of another] does not exist; for the phrase "another" serves to negate what has been previously established, and thus the statement is not intended to imply the existence of an action within itself. Furthermore, since there is no differentiation within the Self, cognition is impossible therein. Moreover, if the Self were an object of cognition, it would follow that there is no cognizer, because it would already be occupied as the object of knowledge.

If it is argued that the single Self exists in both ways—as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and as the knower (*jñātṛ*)—it is not so, because [the Self] is partless (*anaṃśa*). For it is not possible for that which is without parts to simultaneously be both the object of knowledge and the knower. Furthermore, if the Self were an object of cognition like a jar or similar things, the instruction on knowledge would be purposeless; for an instruction on knowledge is not meaningful for that which is already well-established like a jar. Therefore, if it possesses the state of being a knower, its infinity (*ānantya*) cannot be established. Moreover, its being pure existence (*sanmātratva*) is untenable when it possesses specific attributes such as being the agent of knowledge.

And being "pure existence" (sanmātratva) is its reality, according to another Vedic scripture which states, "That is Truth. Therefore, because the word *jñāna* is used as an attribute together with the words "Truth" and "Infinite," the word *jñāna* functions as a noun denoting a state of being (*bhāvasādhana*). The expression "Brahman is knowledge" is employed to negate agency and other such factors of action, as well as to negate the nature of insentience, just as [the term] "clay" [negates the specific forms of pots, etc.]. From the statement "Brahman is knowledge," the quality of finitude might be inferred, since worldly knowledge is observed to be finite.

Therefore, in order to exclude that [misconception], he says "infinite" (*ananta*). Since terms such as "real" (*satya*) have the purpose of negating attributes such as "unreal," and since the qualificand, Brahman, is not well-known—just like a blue lotus and so forth—it might be argued that the statement beginning with "real" results in a purely negative meaning (*śūnyārthatā*), like this: "Here comes the son of a barren woman, having bathed in the waters of a mirage, wearing a crown made of sky-flowers, and bearing a bow made of a hare's horn. [Reply: This is not so, because [the words] serve to define [Brahman].

We have already stated that even though [terms] such as "truth" (satya) function as qualifiers, their primary purpose is to serve as definitions (lakṣaṇa). For if the object to be defined (lakṣya) were empty, the statement of its definition would be meaningless; therefore, because they serve the purpose of defining, we consider them not to have emptiness as their meaning. Furthermore, even when serving as qualifiers, terms such as "truth" do not abandon their own referents. Indeed, if the words "truth" and so forth had emptiness as their meaning, it would be impossible for them to act as restrictors of the qualificand (viśeṣya).

But if [the terms] possess meaning through their referents such as "truth" and so forth, then it is logical that Brahman, the qualificand, possesses the quality of being the controller in contrast to other qualificands that possess qualities opposite to those. The word *brahman* itself is indeed meaningful by virtue of its own primary sense. In this context, the word *ananta* (infinite) functions as a qualifier by means of negating finitude (*antavattva*), whereas the words *satya* (truth) and *jñāna* (knowledge) function as qualifiers precisely by imparting their own respective meanings.

Therefore, from the phrase "from this very Self" (*tasmād vaitasmād ātmanaḥ*), because the word "Self" (*ātman*) is applied to Brahman itself, Brahman is the very Self of the knower. Furthermore, the texts demonstrate its nature as the Self by stating, "He enters this Self consisting of bliss" (*etam ānandamayam ātmānam upasaṅkrāmati*). Moreover, through the teaching of its entry into that [body], in the passage "Having created that, He entered into it," the entry of that very [Brahman] into the body in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) is shown. Thus, Brahman is the true nature of the knower. If this is so, then because it is the Self, it must be the agent of knowledge; for it is well known that "the Self is the knower."

Furthermore, from the statement "He desired," it is well known that the one who desires is the agent of knowledge (*jñāna-kartṛ*). Therefore, it is incorrect to say that Brahman is "mere consciousness" (*jñapti*) on the grounds that it is the agent of knowledge; for this would entail the consequence of its being non-eternal. Even if Brahman were of the nature of an entity (*bhāva-rūpa*) such that "consciousness" (*jñapti*) means "knowledge" (*jñāna*), it would still follow that it is non-eternal and dependent. This is because verbal roots (*dhātu*) require an agent (*kāraka*), and "knowledge" is the meaning of a verbal root. Consequently, it would be non-eternal and subject to dependence.

No, because the designation "effect" is applied [to consciousness] without it being distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*). The nature of the Self is cognition (*jñapti*), and since it is not separate from that, it is indeed eternal. Nevertheless, those appearances in the form of sound and so forth—which belong to the intellect (*buddhi*), characterized as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and undergoing transformation into the form of objects through the doors of the eyes and other senses—become the objects of the Self’s cognition. Even as they arise, they arise already pervaded by the Self’s cognition.

Therefore, those modifications which are manifested by the consciousness of the Self and are denoted by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna)—being the very nature of the elements—are imagined by the undiscriminating to be the attributes of the Self itself, consisting of the form of transformation. But as for the consciousness of Brahman, like the light of the sun or the heat of fire, it is non-different from the essential nature of Brahman; it is that very nature itself. It does not depend on any other cause.

Because all things have an eternal nature, and because [Brahman] is undivided in space and time, because it is the cause of time, space, and so forth, and because of its unsurpassed subtlety, there exists nothing else—whether subtle, hidden, remote, past, present, or future—that is unknowable to it. Therefore, that Brahman is omniscient. And the words of the Mantras declare: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, and He hears without ears."

"He knows the knowable, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the great Puruṣa"—and because of such scriptural passages as, "For there is no loss of the consciousness of the conscious one, owing to its imperishability, nor is there a second thing existing apart from it," and so forth, Brahman's status as the very nature of knowledge is established as eternal, since it is non-different from the nature of the knower and independent of causes such as the instruments of perception. Therefore, it is not the meaning of a verbal root, because it does not consist of the form of an action.

For this very reason, Brahman is not the agent of knowledge, and for that same reason, it is not even denotable by the word "knowledge. Nevertheless, it is indicated—though not directly expressed—by the word "knowledge," which refers to the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*) and serves as its appearance; for Brahman is devoid of the categories such as genus (*jāti*), which are the grounds for the application of words. The same applies to the word "truth" (*satya*). Since the essential nature of Brahman is the total cessation of all particularities, it is indicated by the word "truth"—which has as its object the universal of external existence—as "Brahman is truth."

But Brahman is not merely that which is denoted by the word "truth" (satya). Thus, words such as "truth" and the rest, being mutually restrictive and restricted through their proximity to one another, serve both to exclude [Brahman] from what is denoted by words like "truth" and to function as indicators (lakṣaṇa) for Brahman. Therefore, it is established that Brahman is inexpressible, as stated in the passages: "from which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it," and "unexpounded, without abode. Furthermore, Brahman is not the meaning of a sentence, just as a blue lotus is not.

He who knows—that is, understands—that Brahman as it has been described, which is "hidden," meaning situated in the cave; for the root *guh* means to conceal, and since the categories of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower are concealed within it, the "cave" is the intellect (*buddhi*). Or, it may mean that the two goals of human life—enjoyment and liberation—are hidden within it. In that supreme, most excellent "vault" or space, namely the unmanifested space (*avyākṛta-ākāśa*)—for that is indeed the supreme vault, as it is said, "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, is the space"—it is so called because of its proximity to the Imperishable.

Alternatively, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "in the cave" or "in the ether," the unmanifest ether (*avyākṛtākāśa*) itself is the cave; for even there, all entities are hidden throughout the three periods of time, owing to its being the cause and its extreme subtlety. Within that is deposited Brahman. However, it is more logical that the supreme ether is indeed the ether within the heart (*hārdam*), since the ether is intended here as a subordinate member of knowledge (*vijñāna*).

The supreme nature of the space within the heart is well-established from another Vedic scripture which states: "That which is the space outside a person, that indeed is the space inside a person; that which is the space within the heart. In that space within the heart, there is the intellect, which is the cave; in that [intellect], Brahman is deposited, and it is perceived as distinct through the exclusion of that [intellect]. For otherwise, there could be no connection with a specific place or time for Brahman, because of its omnipresence and its being devoid of distinctions.

Knowing Brahman in this way, what does he [the knower] say? He says: "He enjoys"—that is, he experiences—all desires (*kāmān*), meaning all objects of enjoyment, without exception. Is it like us and others, who experience sons, heaven, and so forth in succession? No; he says: "simultaneously" (*saha*), that is, at once, all having arisen in a single moment through a single perception, which—like the light of the sun—is eternal and non-different from the very nature of Brahman, which we have described as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite. This is what is meant by the phrase "together with Brahman" (*brahmaṇā saha*).

The wise one, having become Brahman, enjoys all desires simultaneously by means of his very nature as Brahman; he does not enjoy all desires—such as those dependent on dharma and other causes, or those dependent on the instruments of the senses like the eyes—as the worldly person does by turns, through a reflected form produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like the reflection of the sun in water.

How then? The meaning is that, in the manner described, by means of the omniscient, omnipresent, and all-pervading nature of the eternal Brahman-Ātman, he enjoys all desires simultaneously—without depending on causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, and without depending on instruments such as the eyes and other senses. "By the wise one" (*vipaścitā*) means by the omniscient one; that which is omniscience is "wisdom" (*vaipaścitya*), and by means of that omniscient nature, he enjoys [them] through Brahman. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra.

The entire meaning of the section on the creeper (*vallī*) was encapsulated by the Brāhmaṇa statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. That meaning, indicated by the aphorism (*sūtra*), has been explained in brief by means of the mantra. Now, since a detailed determination of its meaning must be made, the subsequent portion of the text—which stands in the place of a commentary (*vṛtti*)—is commenced, beginning with the words, "From that, indeed, from this... and so forth.

And in that regard, it was stated at the beginning of the mantra, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. To the question, "How is it both true and infinite? he says: "In that context, infinity is indeed threefold—by way of space, by way of time, and by way of substance. For example, space is infinite by way of space, for there is no spatial limitation of it; however, space is not infinite by way of time nor by way of substance. Why? Because it is an effect.

Brahman is not thus limited by time even as space is, because it is unproduced (*akārya*). For an object that is a product is delimited by time, but Brahman is not a product; therefore, it is infinite even with respect to time. Likewise, it is infinite with respect to substance (*vastu*). How, then, is there infinity with respect to substance? Because it is non-different from everything. For a distinct object constitutes the limit of another object; for the cognition of one object is excluded from another object that is distinct from it.

That from which the cognition of something ceases is its limit (*anta*). For example, since the cognition of "cowness" ceases with respect to "horseness," cowness has horseness as its limit; thus, it possesses a limit. And such a limit is observed among distinct entities, but there is no such differentiation in Brahman. Therefore, Brahman is infinite even in terms of its actual reality (*vastutaḥ*). But how is it said that Brahman is non-different from everything? Because it is the cause of all things. For Brahman is indeed the cause of all things, including time, space, and so forth.

If it is argued that Brahman is actually finite with respect to its effects, we say no; for the state of being an effect is unreal. Indeed, apart from the cause, there is no such thing as an "effect" that exists in reality from which the cognition of the cause could be withdrawn. For another Śruti passage states: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real," and likewise, "Being alone is real. Therefore, because it is the cause of ether and the rest, Brahman is infinite in terms of space.

For it is well known that space is infinite in terms of location (*deśataḥ*), and since this [Self] has that as its cause, the infinity of the Self in terms of location is established. Indeed, nothing is seen in the world arising from something that is not all-pervading (*asarvagata*) to become all-pervading. Therefore, the infinity of the Self in terms of location is unsurpassed; likewise, it is so in terms of time (*kālataḥ*) because it is uncaused, and in terms of substance (*vastutaḥ*) because there exists no other distinct entity apart from it. For this very reason, its truth is unsurpassed.

The word "from that" (*tasmāt*) refers back to Brahman as formulated in the root aphorism; the word "from this" (*etasmāt*) refers to it as it was immediately characterized by the mantra passage. That Brahman which was formulated at the beginning by the Brāhmaṇa passage, and which was characterized immediately thereafter as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite"—from that Brahman, from the Self denoted by the word "Self. For the Self is that of all things, according to another scriptural text: "That is the Truth, that is the Self. Therefore, Brahman is the Self.

From this Brahman, which is the very nature of the Self, space (ākāśa) was produced—that is, it arose. Space is characterized by the quality of sound and provides room for material substances. From that space, wind (vāyu), possessing its own quality of touch along with the prior quality of space—sound—is produced as having two qualities; the word "was produced" is understood to carry over. And from wind, fire (agni), possessing its own quality of form along with the two prior qualities, is produced as having three qualities.

From fire, by means of its own quality of taste and the three preceding qualities, water is produced as having four qualities. From water, by means of its own quality of smell and the four preceding qualities, earth is produced as having five qualities. From earth come plants; from plants comes food; and from food, transformed into the form of semen, the person (puruṣa) is produced, possessing the configuration of a head, hands, and so forth.

This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*)—that is, he is a transformation of the essence of food. For from all the limbs [of the body], the seed (sperm), which is a manifestation of light (*tejas*), is produced in the form of a person; therefore, whoever is born from it must likewise have the form of a person. This is because, among all species, we observe a rule regarding the form of the progenitor in those being born. Although all beings are equally transformations of the essence of food and equally belong to the lineage of Brahman, why is only the "person" (*puruṣa*) specifically mentioned? It is because of his preeminence.

What, then, is this preeminence? It is the qualification for ritual action and knowledge. For it is the person alone—because of his capacity, his desire, and his being unexcluded—who, being both desirous and wise, is qualified for the purpose of ritual action and knowledge. Indeed, in the person alone does the Self reside more fully; for he is most perfectly endowed with wisdom: he speaks what is known, he sees what is known, he knows what is to come, he perceives the worlds and the non-worlds, and through his mortality he beholds the immortal—thus is he endowed.

For we see from other scriptural passages that for other animals, hunger and thirst alone constitute their means of cognition; thus, this person here is intended to be led by knowledge to the innermost Brahman. Since his intellect has habitually identified with external forms that are not the Self, it is impossible to suddenly make it turn toward the innermost inward Self without a support and without an object—just as in the illustration of the moon seen through a tree branch. Therefore, by means of the conceptualization of the similarity between the perceived body and the Self, [the mind is directed] inward.

Introducing [the next section], he says: "This indeed is its head. Of this person consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*), this is the well-known head. The phrase "this indeed is the head" is stated so that the same designation might not be mistakenly applied here as well, given that in the cases of the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) and the others, no head is observed. The application of the terms is to be understood in the same way for the wings and other parts: this right arm of the person facing east is the right wing; this left arm is the northern wing.

This middle portion of the body is the *ātman*, for according to the Vedic scripture, "the *ātman* is indeed the center of these limbs. That limb which is below the navel is the tail, the support (*pratiṣṭhā*). It is called the support because one stands firm by means of it. It is like a tail due to the common characteristic of hanging downward, just as the tail of a cow.
