From food, which has undergone transformation into the state of sap and so forth—the word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of recollection—creatures, both stationary and moving, are born. Whatever creatures there are that are undistinguished and dependent upon the earth, all of them are born from food alone. Moreover, once born, they live by food alone; that is to say, they maintain their vital breaths and grow. Furthermore, they dissolve into this very food; the word "api" (into) has the sense of "prati" (towards). The meaning is that they are absorbed back into food.

"In the end" means at the conclusion of life, which is characterized by its activity. Why? Because food (*anna*) is the "eldest," meaning the first-born, of all beings—that is, of living creatures. For food is the cause of the other beings, such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth. Therefore, all progeny originate from food, subsist on food, and dissolve into food. And because this is so, food is called the "universal medicine" (*sarvauṣadha*), for it pacifies the burning of the bodies of all living beings.

The fruit for those who know food as Brahman is now stated: they indeed obtain the entire aggregate of all that is born of food. Who are they? Those who meditate upon food as Brahman, as described. How? [Thinking: "I am born of food, my self is food, and my dissolution is in food; therefore, food is Brahman. But why does meditation on the self as food result in the attainment of all food? It is said: "For food is the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*) among beings. Because it was produced before all beings, it is the eldest; and because it is the eldest, it is called the "all-healer" (*sarvauṣadha*).

Therefore, for one who meditates upon the Self as all food, the attainment of all food is logically established. The statement that "beings are born from food, and once born, they grow through food" is repeated for the purpose of providing a conclusion. Now, the etymological derivation of "food" (*anna*) is stated: "That which is eaten (*adyate*) and consumed by beings, and which itself eats and consumes beings—for that reason, because it is consumed by beings and because it is the consumer of beings, it is called 'food' (*anna*). The word "iti" marks the completion of the first sheath (*kośa*).

Desiring to show, through knowledge, that Brahman—which is the innermost of all selves beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), the scripture introduces it by means of removing the five sheaths created by ignorance, just as one reveals the rice grains within by husking out the many layers of the *kodrava* grain; thus it begins: "Now, from this very one consisting of the essence of food," and so forth.

Therefore, distinct from and separate from this aforementioned body composed of the essence of food, there is another, inner, internal self (*ātman*)—just like the physical body—which is falsely imagined as the self and consists of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*). "Vital breath" (*prāṇa*) is wind; it consists of that, meaning it is predominantly made of that. This self composed of the essence of food is filled by that self composed of vital breath, just as a leather bag is filled with air. Indeed, this self composed of vital breath is also shaped like a person (*puruṣavidha*), having the form of a person with a head, wings, and so forth. Is it so by its own nature? No, he says:

The fact that the self consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) has the form of a person is well known. Following the person-like nature—that is, the human shape—of that self consisting of the essence of food, the self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) also becomes person-like; it does not possess this shape inherently, but rather like a cast image from a mold. In this way, following the person-like nature of each preceding self, each subsequent one becomes person-like, and each preceding one is filled by each subsequent one.

How, then, is its anthropomorphic form described? Of that *prāṇamaya*—which is a modification of air—the *prāṇa* itself is the head; that is, the specific function (*vṛtti*) of the *prāṇa* which issues from the mouth and nostrils is figuratively conceived as the head, because of the scriptural statement. In all cases, the conception of the wings and other parts arises solely from scriptural statement. The *vyāna*, the function of the *vyāna*, is the right wing. The *apāna* is the left wing.

Space is the self (*ātman*). That specific function (*vṛttiviśeṣa*) residing in space, called "the equal" (*samāna*), is the self; it is the self because it presides over the function of breath (*prāṇa*), and because, being situated in the middle with respect to the other peripheral functions, it is the self. For it is well-known from scripture that "the self is the center of these limbs," establishing that what is situated in the middle is the self. Earth is the tail, the support. By "earth" is meant the deity Earth, who is the sustainer of the internal breath (*prāṇa*) because she is the cause of its stability.

"This very [earth] supports the downward breath (apāna) of the person," for so says another scriptural passage. Otherwise, due to its weight, the body would either move upward through the function of the upward breath (udāna) or fall down. Therefore, the deity Earth is the tail, the support of the self consisting of breath (prāṇamaya). With reference to that very same subject—the self consisting of breath—there is this verse:

The gods breathe after the breath (*prāṇa*); so do humans and animals. For the breath is the life-span (*āyus*) of beings; therefore it is called "the whole life-span. Those who meditate upon the breath as Brahman attain their full life-span. For the breath is the life-span of beings; therefore it is called "the whole life-span. This is indeed its embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), which is the same as that of the preceding [sheath]. Now, different from this one consisting of breath is another inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya*). By that, this [sheath] is filled.

Verily, this [Brahman] is of the very form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). Following its person-like form, he [the individual soul] is of the form of a person. Of that [Brahman], the Yajus is the head; the Ṛk is the right wing; the Sāman is the left wing; the Instruction (*ādeśa*) is the body (*ātman*); and the Atharvāṅgirases are the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse: Thus ends the third Anuvāka. 3.

"The gods breathe after the breath. The gods—Agni and the others—breathe after the breath, that is, after the wind-self which possesses the power of breathing; having become one with it, they breathe, they perform the act of breathing, and through the activity of breathing, they become possessed of action. Alternatively, because this section concerns the internal self (*adhyātma*), "the gods" refers to the sense organs; they breathe after the breath, meaning they move in accordance with the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). Likewise, humans and animals are those who possess movement only through the act of breathing.

Therefore, living beings do not possess a self consisting only of the limited self made of food (*annamaya*). What then? Human beings and others possess a self also through that which is contained within it—the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath)—which is common to all and pervades every body. In this way, all living beings possess a self through the subsequent, subtler selves beginning with the *manomaya* (consisting of mind), ending with the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), which are composed of the elements starting with space (*ākāśa*), are successively more pervasive than their predecessors, and are produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Likewise, they possess the Self through that which is innate—the eternal, unchanging, all-pervading cause of space and so forth, characterized by truth, knowledge, and infinity, transcending the five sheaths, and being the Self of all. For it is also implied by the sense of the matter that He alone is, in the ultimate sense, the Self of all. As for the statement, "The gods breathe after the breath," he asks why this is so and says: because the breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the life-force, the very living, of all beings who possess breath.

For, according to another Vedic text, "As long as the vital breath (prāṇa) dwells in this body, so long is there life. Therefore, it is "all-life" (sarvāyuṣam). The life of all is "all-life" (sarvāyuḥ), and that which is all-life is called "all-life" (sarvāyuṣam). This is because death is universally recognized to occur upon the departure of the vital breath; for the status of the vital breath as "all-life" is indeed well-known in the world.

Therefore, having stepped out from this external, non-common *annamaya* self, those who worship the internal, common *prāṇamaya* self as Brahman—thinking, "I am the *prāṇa*, the self of all beings, because I am the cause of life and longevity"—they attain the full span of life in this world; they do not die an untimely death before reaching their allotted lifespan. This is the meaning. As for the phrase "a hundred years," however, it is more appropriate [to understand it as] "one attains the whole of life," since that is well-known in the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).

What is the reason? For *prāṇa* is the life-span (*āyus*) of living beings; therefore, it is called "the whole life-span" (*sarvāyuṣa*). The statement beginning with "For *prāṇa*... is repeated for the purpose of establishing the cause for attaining the fruit of knowledge—that whoever meditates upon Brahman as possessing certain qualities becomes a partaker of those very qualities. Of that preceding *annamaya*, this very *prāṇamaya* is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) existing within the *annamaya* body. Who is he? He who is this *prāṇamaya*. The rest, beginning with "From him indeed," has already been explained. Another inner self is the *manomaya*.

"Mind" (*manas*) refers to the internal organ consisting of volition and the like; that which consists of this is "mind-made" (*manomaya*). This is the self within the vital-breath-self (*prāṇamaya*). Of this [self], the *yajus* alone is the head. By "yajus" is meant a particular type of mantra whose syllables, feet, and terminations are not fixed; the word *yajus* here denotes that class [of mantras]. Its status as the head is due to its preeminence. Its preeminence arises because it provides direct assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāra*) in sacrifices and the like; for by means of the *yajus*, along with the utterance of *svāhā* and so forth, the oblation is offered. Or rather, the conceptualization of the head and other parts is based on scriptural injunction (*vācanikī*), as is the case everywhere.

For the mental modification (*vṛtti*)—which has as its objects the place, effort, intonation, sound, syllable, word, and sentence; which consists of the resolve (*saṅkalpa*) toward those [objects]; which is cultivated by them; and which is distinguished by the convention (*saṅketa*) of the *Yajus*—is called "the *Yajus*" when it proceeds through the doors of the sense organs such as the ear. Likewise for the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman*. And thus, since the mantras are mental modifications, it is the modification itself that is repeated; therefore, mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*) is logically established. Otherwise, because it would not be an object [of the senses], the mantra could not be repeated, just like a jar or similar objects, and thus mental recitation would not be possible.

Furthermore, the repetition of a mantra is enjoined many times in ritual acts. If it is argued that the repetition of the mantra occurs through the repetition of the memory directed toward its syllables, we say no; for the primary meaning [of the injunction] would be impossible. In the passage, "He recites the first verse three times, he recites the last verse three times," the repetition of the *ṛc* (verse) is heard. In that context, if the *ṛc* were not the object [of the injunction], and if repetition were performed merely through a memory directed toward it, then the primary meaning enjoined—the repetition of the *ṛc* itself as expressed by "he recites the first verse three times"—would be abandoned.

Therefore, the self-consciousness—which is delimited by the limiting adjuncts of mental modifications (*manovṛtti-upādhi*), which is grounded in mental modifications, and which is without beginning or end—is denoted by the word *yajus*; these are the *mantras*. In this way, the eternity of the Vedas is established. Otherwise, if they were objects [of cognition], they would be non-eternal like color-form (*rūpa*) and other such things. This is not tenable. Furthermore, the Śruti passage, "That wherein all the Vedas become one—that is the Self within the mind" (*mānasīna ātmā*), speaking of the oneness of the eternal Self, would be consistent only if the *Ṛk* and other Vedas are eternal.

And there is this Vedic verse: "In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, all the gods have taken their seat. Here, the *ādeśa* (instruction) refers to the Brāhmaṇas, because they instruct regarding the specific things to be taught. The mantras and Brāhmaṇas seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras constitute the tail, the foundation, because they primarily consist of rites for pacification, nourishment, and other such acts that serve as the basis for ritual establishment. Regarding that, there is also this verse which elucidates the self consisting of mind, as before.

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—he who knows that bliss of Brahman, never fears at any time. Of that [bliss], this very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), which belongs to the former [the *vijñānamaya*]. From this, indeed, from that which consists of mind (*manomaya*), there is another inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). By that, this [self] is filled. That very one is indeed of the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). Following its person-like form, this [self] is also of the form of a person. Of that, faith (*śraddhā*) alone is the head; truth (*ṛta*) is the right wing.
Truth is the head; Yoga is the self; Greatness is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse: (TaittU 2.4.1).
Thus ends the fourth section. 4.

"From which words turn back, not having attained [it] along with the mind," and so forth. Of that preceding one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), this very one is the embodied self (*śārīra*); "embodied" means existing within the body consisting of breath. Which one? This one which consists of mind (*manomaya*). "From him, indeed, from this one," and so forth, is as before. There is another inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), which is internal to the one consisting of mind; the one consisting of mind has been described as the self of the Vedas.

Vijñāna is the intellect whose object is the meaning of the Vedas and which consists of certainty; it is a quality of the internal organ characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*). That which is composed of this—whose self is brought about by certainties and cognitions that are themselves the nature of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—is the *vijñānamaya*. For sacrifices and other rites are performed preceded by such cognitive means of valid knowledge. And he will state in a subsequent verse that [this sheath] is the cause of sacrifice and so forth. Indeed, for one who possesses certain cognition, faith first arises regarding those things that ought to be done.

It is the "head" because it is the foremost among all things to be accomplished, just as the head is for the body. *Ṛta* and *satya* are exactly as previously explained. *Yoga* means application, concentration, or mental composure. It is the "self" (*ātman*). For when one possesses the self—meaning when one is disciplined and composed—the limbs such as faith and the rest become capable of attaining the true goal, just like the limbs of a person who has a self. Therefore, concentration (*samādhāna*) or yoga is the self of that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). *Mahaḥ* (the Great) is the tail, the support. *Mahaḥ* refers to the principle of Greatness (*mahattattva*), which is the first-born.

"Great is the Yakṣa, the first-born," according to another Vedic text. The "tail" is the support because it is the cause; for the cause is indeed the support of its effects, just as the earth is the support of trees and creepers. And the Great Principle (mahattattva) is the cause of all cognitions; therefore, it is the support of the self consisting of cognition. Regarding this, there is also the following verse, as before—just as there were verses illuminating the selfs consisting of food and so forth mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa, so too is there one for the self consisting of cognition. 4.

"Consciousness performs the sacrifice; it also performs ritual acts. All the gods worship consciousness as the eldest Brahman. If one knows consciousness to be Brahman, and if one does not become negligent because of that, having cast off all evils from the body, one enjoys all desires. This is its very self within the body, which is the same as the self of the preceding [sheath]. Now, different from this self consisting of consciousness is another inner self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). By that [self], this [self of consciousness] is filled. And this [self of bliss] is indeed of the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*).

Following its human form, it is itself human in form. Its head is joy (*priya*); its right wing is delight (*moda*); its left wing is extreme delight (*pramoda*); its self (*ātman*) is bliss (*ānanda*); Brahman is its tail, its support. On this point there is also this verse: Thus ends the fifth section (Anuvāka). 5.1.5.1. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1)

Consciousness performs the sacrifice; for it is one possessed of consciousness who performs the sacrifice, preceded by faith and other such qualities. Therefore, consciousness has the status of an agent, as expressed by the phrase "it performs. It also performs actions. Since everything has consciousness as its agent, it is logical that the Self consisting of consciousness is Brahman.

Furthermore, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is Brahman; all the gods, beginning with Indra, worship—that is, they meditate upon—Brahman as the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*), because it is the first-born due to its being the precursor of all activities. The meaning is that they worship by forming an identification with that Brahman consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). Therefore, through the worship of the Great Brahman, they become possessed of knowledge and sovereignty.

And if one knows—that is, understands—that this consciousness is Brahman, not only does one know it, but if one does not become negligent toward that Brahman—negligent by habitually identifying the Self with external non-Self objects—then such negligence regarding the cultivation of the sense of Self within Brahman, which consists of consciousness, would be expected; therefore, to prevent that, it is said: "if one does not become negligent toward it."

The meaning is: if one does not remain while contemplating the state of the Self in the pure Brahman consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), having abandoned the sense of self in the [sheaths] beginning with that consisting of food (*annamaya*). What would happen then? It is said: "having cast off evils from the body. For all evils have their cause in the identification with the body; when that cause ceases—due to the identification with the Self in the Brahman consisting of consciousness—their abandonment becomes possible, just as shade disappears when the umbrella is removed.

Therefore, having abandoned all evils—which have their cause in the conceit of the body and originate from the body—right within the body itself, one who has attained the true nature of the Brahman consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) fully enjoys, that is, perfectly partakes of, all desires residing therein by means of the self consisting of consciousness alone. Of that former [self] consisting of mind (*manomaya*), this very one is the "bodily" (*śārīra*) self, existing within the body consisting of mind. Who is he? He is this one consisting of consciousness. The phrase "from that, or from this" has its meaning already explained.

The understanding that the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is an effect-self arises from both the context and the word *mayaṭ*. For here, the effect-selves composed of food and so forth—the elemental beings—are the subject under discussion; and this "consisting of bliss" falls within that same context. Furthermore, the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen here in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), as in the case of "consisting of food" (*annamaya*). Therefore, the "consisting of bliss" should be understood as an effect-self. Moreover, because of the transition, the text will later state: "He approaches the self consisting of bliss."

Furthermore, the transition of things consisting of effects is observed to occur by means of things consisting of food; and the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is heard of in scripture as the object of the act of transition, as in the passage, "He transitions into the Self consisting of food. Nor can there be a transition into the Self itself, because that would contradict the context and is impossible. For it is not possible for the Self to transition into the Self, since there is no division within the Self. Moreover, Brahman is the very nature of the one who transitions, and thus the conceptualization of [Brahman] having a head and so forth is untenable.

For indeed, the figurative attribution of limbs such as a head and so forth is not possible in a cause such as space (ākāśa), which possesses the characteristics already described and does not fall within the category of an effect. This is because of scriptural passages that negate specific attributes, such as: "It is unseen, bodiless, unexplained, without abode; It is neither gross nor subtle, not this, not that" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26); and because of the impossibility of citing a mantra [in support of such an interpretation]. For there would be no possibility of the doubt, "Brahman does not exist," regarding Brahman as the Self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) when it is being directly experienced as qualified by limbs such as a dear head.

The citation of the mantra, "If one knows that Brahman is non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent," is thus appropriate. Furthermore, the separate mention of Brahman as the "tail, the support" (brahma pucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā) would otherwise be untenable. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is merely one who has fallen into the realm of effects, and not the supreme Self itself. "Bliss" (ānanda) is the fruit of knowledge and action; that which is composed of it is the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). And this is internal to the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), because scripture declares its internality relative to the one consisting of consciousness, which has sacrifice and other such acts as its cause.

For the fruit of knowledge and action must be most proximate to the enjoyer, since it exists for the sake of the enjoyer; and the self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is more proximate than the preceding ones. Furthermore, knowledge and action are for the sake of the pleasant and so forth (*priyādi*); indeed, knowledge and action are prompted by the pleasant and its like. Therefore, because the pleasant and other fruits are in close proximity to the Self, it is logical that this [self of bliss] is more internal than the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). For the self consisting of bliss—which is produced from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the pleasant and so forth—is perceived in dreams as resting upon the self consisting of consciousness.

Of that self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), "dear" (*priya*)—born from the sight of a beloved son or the like—is the head, as it were, because of its preeminence. "Joy" (*moda*) is the exhilaration caused by the acquisition of what is dear. That same exhilaration when intensified is "delight" (*pramoda*). "Bliss" (*ānanda*) is the general state of happiness, which is the self (*ātman*) of the constituent parts of happiness such as the "dear," because it is woven through them all. "Bliss" (*ānanda*) is the Supreme Brahman.

For when that [pleasure] is presented by virtuous action (*śubhakarma*) within a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttiviśeṣa*) conditioned by particular objects such as sons or friends—and is not obscured by darkness (*tamas*)—it becomes manifest in its clarity. This is what is well-known in the world as "the pleasure of that object. Because the action that presents that specific modification of the internal organ is not permanent, pleasure is momentary (*kṣaṇikatva*).

Thus, to the extent that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) attains purity through austerity that destroys darkness, through knowledge, celibacy, and faith—to that same extent, as the internal organ becomes solitary and serene, a particular excellence of bliss (*ānanda-viśeṣa*) is elevated and expanded. And it will be said [in the scripture]: "He is indeed the essence (*rasa*); for having obtained this essence, one becomes joyful... for he alone causes bliss; other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss," according to another scriptural passage.

And thus, with reference to the progressive excellence of the cessation of desires, an increase of bliss by a factor of one hundred at each successive stage will be described. And so, with respect to the knowledge of the supreme Brahman—the very Brahman under discussion which is characterized as Truth, Knowledge, and Infinity, for the sake of whose realization the five sheaths consisting of food and the rest were introduced, which is more internal than those, and by which all of them possess their self—that Brahman is the tail, the foundation.

And that very non-dual Brahman, which is the ultimate limit of all duality imagined through ignorance, is the foundation; for it is the culmination of the unity of that which consists of bliss. That one non-dual Brahman, the ultimate limit of duality imagined through ignorance, exists as the foundation and the tail. Regarding this very point, there is this verse:

"He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent; but if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. This very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of the former [the Self consisting of bliss]. Now, therefore, follow these questions: Does anyone who is ignorant go to that world after departing? Or does anyone who is wise attain that world after departing? He desired: "May I become many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he created all this.

"Whatever there is—having created that, it entered into it. Having entered it, it became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*); the defined and the undefined; the founded and the unfounded; consciousness and non-consciousness; the real and the unreal. Whatever there is—that is what they call the Real (*satya*). On this point, there is also this verse: (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1). Thus ends the sixth section. 6.

It is indeed non-existent, exactly like that which is non-existent; just as that which is non-existent has no connection with human goals (*puruṣārtha*), so too does that [Brahman] become unconnected with human goals. Which one is this? If someone knows—that is, understands—that Brahman is non-existent and not present; or, conversely, if someone knows that "that Brahman exists," even though it is the locus of all conceptual constructions, the seed of all activity, and the cessation of all particularity—then how can there be any doubt regarding its non-existence? We reply: because Brahman transcends all empirical discourse.

For when the intellect is habituated to existence regarding that which belongs to the sphere of empirical usage—being merely a verbal handle—it likewise apprehends non-existence regarding its opposite, that which transcends empirical usage. Just as it is well known that a jar or the like, being established as an object of empirical usage, is "existent," while its opposite is "non-existent," so too, by analogy with that, there might arise here a suspicion of the non-existence of Brahman. Therefore, it is said: "If one knows that Brahman exists..."

What, then, would happen for one who knows that "it exists"? To this he says: the knowers of Brahman recognize such a person—who is existent (*santam*), present as the very nature of Brahman, and has attained the Self that is real in the ultimate sense—as one who possesses this knowledge. Therefore, from that realization of its existence, he becomes for others to be known as being like Brahman; this is the meaning.

Alternatively, he who thinks "Brahman does not exist" arrives at the non-existence of the entire path of righteousness—characterized by the established order of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*)—due to his lack of faith, since that [path] exists for the purpose of realizing Brahman. Therefore, such a nihilist (*nāstika*) is called "non-existent" and "unrighteous" in the world.

He who knows that "Brahman exists" as being the opposite of that [ignorance]—because he, through faith, correctly follows that true path characterized by the established order of castes, stages of life, and so forth, which is the means for attaining that Brahman—therefore the virtuous know him to be a "sādhuh," one who stands upon the path of the good. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that Brahman must indeed be understood as "it exists. Of that former self consisting of knowledge (vijñānamaya), this very one existing in the body consisting of knowledge is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā).

Who is this? It is this one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Regarding him, there is no doubt as to his non-existence; however, because Brahman is devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), a doubt concerning its non-existence is appropriate, as is the case with Brahman due to its universal sameness (*sāmya*). Since this is so, therefore, immediately after that, the "subsequent questions" (*anupraśna*)—that is, those questions which follow upon the words of the teacher—are for the sake of the listener, the disciple. For Brahman is common to both the knower and the ignorant, since it is the cause of ether and the rest.

Therefore, the attainment of Brahman by even the ignorant person is questioned: "Does even the ignorant one—*uta api avidvān*—having departed from here, go to—that is, reach—that world, the Supreme Self? The word *cana* has the sense of *api*. Or does he not go? A second question is also to be understood here, because of the plural number in the term "subsequent questions" (*anupraśnāḥ*).

Two further questions concern the wise man: if even the ignorant person does not go to Brahman, which is the common cause, then one might suspect that even the wise man does not go to Brahman; therefore, a question is asked regarding him: "Or the wise man? By drawing down the syllable *u* from the word *uta* to be mentioned later and joining the syllable *ta* from the preceding word *uta*, and by placing the word *uta* before the word *aho*, he asks: "Or rather, the wise man? (*utāho vidvān*).

"Does even some wise person, though a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), after departing from here, attain—that is, reach—that world? *Samaśnute u*—this being the form established, when the substitution of *ay* and the elision of *y* have been made, there is the prolation (*pluti*) of the vowel *a*, resulting in *samaśnutā3 u*. Does the wise person attain that world? Or rather, is there another question: does even the wise person not attain it, just as the ignorant one does not? Or perhaps there are two questions concerning the wise and the ignorant respectively."

The plural number, however, is appropriate with reference to other questions that are implied by the context. From the scriptural statements, "If he knows Brahman as non-existent" and "If he knows Brahman as existent," there arises the doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist; hence, the first secondary question, which follows from this meaning, is: "Does it exist or does it not exist? Because Brahman is impartial, the second [question] is: "Does the ignorant one go [to it] or not? Even though Brahman is equal [to all], one might suspect that just like the ignorant person, the knower also does not go; thus, the third secondary question is: "Does the knower attain [Brahman] or does he not attain it?"

To provide an answer to these [objections], the subsequent portion of the text is commenced. Therein, first of all, existence itself is stated. Furthermore, regarding that which was said—"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite"—it must be explained how its truthfulness consists; this is what is now stated. By the very mention of "existence" (sattva), truthfulness is expressed. For it has been said: "Only that which exists is the Truth. Therefore, by the very mention of existence, truthfulness is expressed.

How is this meaning of this text understood? From the sequence of the words; for the subsequent sentences are indeed connected with this very meaning: "They declare that to be true wherein this space is not bliss," and so forth. In this regard, it is suspected that Brahman is non-existent. Why? Because that which exists is perceived through its specific characteristics, such as a jar or the like; whereas that which does not exist is not perceived, such as a hare's horn or the like. Likewise, Brahman is not perceived.

"Therefore, because it is not perceived as distinct, Brahman does not exist"—that is not so. Because Brahman is the cause of space and the rest, Brahman is not non-existent. Why? For all effects, beginning with space, are perceived as having arisen from Brahman. And in the world, it is observed that whatever arises from something exists, just as clay, seeds, and so forth are the causes of jars, sprouts, and the like. Therefore, because it is the cause of space and the rest, Brahman exists. Furthermore, no effect is ever perceived in the world that has arisen from what is non-existent.

If the effect, such as name and form, were non-existent, it would not be perceived because of its lack of self-nature (*nirātmakatva*); yet it is indeed perceived. Therefore, Brahman exists. Furthermore, if the effect were non-existent, even when it is apprehended, it would be permeated by non-existence; but this is not the case. Therefore, Brahman exists. In this regard, another scriptural passage—“How could the existent be born from the non-existent?”—logically explains the impossibility of the birth of the existent from the non-existent. Consequently, it is logical that Brahman is indeed existent.

If it were a cause like clay, seed, and so forth, then it would be insentient. But this is not so, because it possesses the quality of desiring (*kāmayitṛtva*). For in the world, there is nothing that desires which is insentient. We have already stated that Brahman is omniscient; therefore, its possession of the quality of desiring is logically established. If it is argued that, because it desires, it must have unfulfilled desires like those of ourselves and others, we say no, because of its independence. Desires do not impel Brahman in the same way that defects such as desire impel others by subjecting them to external control.

How, then, is it so? Because they are characterized by the knowledge of truth and are pure due to being identical with its own self, Brahman is not impelled by them; rather, it is Brahman that impels them in accordance with the karma of living beings. Therefore, Brahman possesses independence regarding desires; hence, Brahman is not one whose desires are unfulfilled. This is also because it does not depend on any other means.

Furthermore, whereas for others desires depend on external signs such as objects that are not their own self, and depend on other means consisting of instruments and effects distinct from their own self, Brahman does not have such dependence on signs and the like. Rather, they are non-different from its own self. This is what is stated: "He desired. That Self, from which space was produced, desired—that is, He willed. How? "May I be many; may I become manifold, abundant."

How can there be multiplicity when one [entity] enters into other objects? It is said: "I shall be born," "I shall arise. For this becoming many is not like the birth of a son, which has as its object something distinct from oneself. How then? It is through the manifestation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that reside within the Self but were previously unmanifest. When name-and-form, which reside within the Self, are manifested, they are manifested by Brahman—without abandoning their own essential nature (*svarūpa*)—in all states, with space and time undivided from Brahman.

This differentiation of name and form is the becoming manifold of Brahman; otherwise, it would not be possible for the partless Brahman to undergo multiplicity or limitation, just as the limitation or multiplicity of space is caused solely by other entities. Therefore, the Self becomes manifold only through that [differentiation]. Indeed, there exists no entity other than the Self—whether non-self, separated in space and time, subtle, hidden, distant, past, present, or future.

Therefore, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in all their states have Brahman as their self; it is not that Brahman has them as its essence. Since they do not exist at all if Brahman is excluded, they are said to have Brahman as their essence. And through these two limiting adjuncts (upādhi), Brahman participates in all worldly transactions, such as the knower, the known, knowledge, words, and their meanings.

He, being thus desirous of a self, performed austerity (*tapas*). "Austerity" here refers to knowledge, according to another Vedic text which states, "His austerity consists of knowledge. Since his desires were already fulfilled, austerity of the ordinary kind was simply impossible for him. He performed that austerity; the meaning is that the Self engaged in reflection concerning the arrangement of the world to be created and other such matters.

Having reflected thus and performed austerity, he created—indeed, he brought forth—all this world, which corresponds to the causes such as the karma of living beings, and which is experienced by all living beings in all their states according to their respective experiences, in terms of place, time, name, and form. Whatever this is—that is, whatever exists without distinction—it is said that after creating this world, what did he do? He entered into that very world he had created.

In this regard, the following must be considered: how did he enter? Did the Creator enter by that very same self, or by another? What, first of all, is logical? Since the suffix *ktvā* is heard [in the text], it is logical that he who is the Creator entered himself. But is this not illogical, since if Brahman is the cause like clay, the effect consists of that very essence; for it is the cause itself that transforms into the form of the effect?

Therefore, since the effect has already arisen even before [the cause] has entered, it is illogical for the cause to enter again separately afterwards. For there is no entry of clay into the jar apart from its transformation into the jar. If it is argued that just as clay enters the jar in the form of powder, so too does the Self enter the effect consisting of name and form by means of this [individual] self—this is not tenable because of the oneness of Brahman, as supported by another scriptural passage: "Having entered by means of this living self. Such a view is not logical due to the unity of Brahman.

However, because clay is manifold in nature and possesses parts, it is logical for clay to enter into a jar in the form of powder; this is also because there exists a portion of the clay-powder that has not yet entered. But since the Self is one and partless, and because there is no unoccupied space for it to enter, such entry is not possible. How, then, could there be entry? And yet, entry is indeed logical, because it is stated in scripture: "It entered into that very [being]. Let it be, then, that the Self possesses parts.

If it is argued that, because [the Self] possesses parts, its entry into the effects of name and form is logical—just as the hand enters the mouth—we say no, because there is no empty space [left]. For when [the Self] has transformed into the nature of the effect, there is no region devoid of the Self apart from the effects of name and form into which the individual self (jīvātman) could enter. Furthermore, if it were to enter the cause itself, it would abandon its status as an individual self, just as a jar abandons its jar-ness upon entering the clay.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "He entered into that very [effect]," it is not logical for the cause to enter [into its own effect]. If it is argued that this implies the production of a different effect altogether, we reply: no, because of the contradiction with the statement, "He entered into that very [effect]. If one were to claim that the effect in the form of the individual soul (jīvātman), having undergone the transformation into name and form, becomes a different effect, this is not so, due to the contradiction. For a jar does not become another jar; moreover, it would contradict the scriptural texts on distinction (*vyatireka-śruti*), which reiterate the distinction between the individual soul and the effects of name and form. Thus, such an interpretation would conflict with those scriptures.

Furthermore, liberation would be impossible upon falling into that [state], for one who is being liberated from something does not fall into that very same thing—just as a thief or the like who is bound by a chain does not fall into the chain itself. If it is argued that [Brahman] has transformed through a distinction between external and internal—that the cause, Brahman itself, has transformed into the substratum such as the body and so forth externally, and into the supported individual self (*jīvātman*) within—it is not so; for the entry of that which is already outside is logically untenable. Indeed, that which is already situated inside something is not said to have "entered" that very thing.

The entry of that which is already outside would be an entry [into itself], since such is the observed meaning of the word "entry," as in the expression, "having built a house, he entered it. If it is argued that the entry is like the reflection of the sun in water and so forth, we say no; because [the Self] is unlimited and formless. The appearance of reflections such as the sun in things like water—which possess the nature of clarity—occurs when there is something else that is limited and material. But this is not the case for the Self, because the Self, the cause of space and the rest, is formless and all-pervading.

Furthermore, because there is no other distinct substance that could serve as the locus for a reflection at a distant place, entry in the manner of a reflection is not logical. If this is so, then there is no entry at all, yet we do not perceive any other possibility, given the Vedic revelation: "He entered into that very [being]. And scripture is the cause for the arising of cognition regarding objects beyond the senses; yet, despite our efforts, no such cognition arises from this statement.

"Well then, since it is meaningless, this sentence—'Having created that, he entered into it alone'—should be rejected. No, because it has another purpose. Why this misplaced deliberation? For there is another intended meaning for this sentence which is under discussion; that must be remembered: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; [Brahman is] Truth, Knowledge, Infinite, hidden in the cave of the heart. And the knowledge of That is what is intended, and that is the subject at hand.

For the sake of comprehending the true nature of Brahman, the entire field of effects—beginning with space and ending with that which consists of food (*annamaya*)—has been presented, and the comprehension of Brahman has thus been commenced. Within this context, the self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) is shown to be distinct from the self consisting of food; within that, the self consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) are presented, leading one into the cave of the intellect (*vijñānaguhā*). Therein, the specific self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is revealed. Beyond this, by means of attaining the characteristic marks of the self consisting of supreme bliss, the Self is reached as the ultimate limit of the expansion of bliss.

"Brahman is the tail, the support"—it is to be realized within this very cave (*guhā*) as the non-conceptual ground of all conceptual constructions; thus, entry into it is prescribed. For Brahman is not perceived elsewhere, due to its being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*). Indeed, a connection with a distinguishing attribute (*viśeṣa*) is observed to be the cause of perception, just as Rāhu’s connection with the distinguishing attributes of the moon and the sun [is the cause of perceiving them]. Likewise, the connection between the self and the cave of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-guhā*) is the cause of the perception of Brahman.

Because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possesses the nature of illumination due to its proximity [to the Self], just as the perception of a jar or similar object is characterized by light, so too the perception of the Self must be characterized by the light of the cognitive state (buddhipratyaya). Therefore, the phrase "hidden in the cave" refers precisely to that which is the cause of perception. However, here, with reference to the locus of its activity, it is further stated: "Having created that, He entered into it."

That very same cause, having created this effect beginning with space, has entered into it, as it were, within the cave of the intellect (*buddhi*), and is perceived as possessing specific attributes such as the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the knower. That indeed is its "entry. Therefore, that causal Brahman exists; because it exists, it should be perceived as "it exists. Having entered into that effect, what did it become? It became both the manifest (*sat*), which is the formed (*mūrta*), and the unmanifest (*tyat*), which is the formless (*amūrta*).

For the manifest and the unmanifest, which consist of names and forms that have not yet been differentiated, are differentiated by the Self through the Self residing within them. Once differentiated, they are designated by the terms "manifest" and "unmanifest"; however, because they are not spatially or temporally distinct from the Self, it is said that "the Self became those two. Furthermore, there is the defined and the undefined: the "defined" (nirukta) is that which has been extracted from homogeneous and heterogeneous things and specified as "this is that" by way of particular place and time; the "undefined" (anirukta) is the opposite of that.

The "defined" (*nirukta*) and "undefined" (*anirukta*) are also merely qualifications of the "formed" (*mūrta*) and "formless" (*amūrta*). Just as "existent" (*sat*) and "that" (*tyat*) refer to the perceptible and the imperceptible, so too do "having a dwelling" (*nilayana*) and "not having a dwelling" (*anilayana*). "Having a dwelling"—meaning a nest or a support—is a quality belonging only to the formed; "not having a dwelling," being its opposite, is a quality belonging only to the formless. Although "that" (*tyat*), the "undefined" (*anirukta*), and "not having a dwelling" (*anilayana*) share the nature of being qualities of the formless, they nevertheless pertain exclusively to the realm of the manifested (*vyākṛta*), because it is heard that they exist subsequent to the process of creation.

"Tyat" (That) refers to that which is unmanifested, such as the vital breaths and so forth; it is also that which has no abode. Therefore, these qualifiers refer only to the unmanifested [Brahman] as it pertains to the realm of the manifested. "Vijñāna" (consciousness) means sentience; "avijñāna" (non-consciousness) means that which is devoid of it, such as insentient stones and the like. "Satya" (truth) here refers to that which is within the scope of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), not absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*), because of the context. For Brahman alone is the absolute truth. Here, however, "satya" is relative, referring to water and the like, which are called "true" in comparison to falsehoods such as a mirage.

And untruth is the opposite of that. But what is all this? It is truth, which is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). And what is that? Brahman. For it has been stated in the context: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."

Since this entire collection of modifications—consisting of the class of things denoted by "Being" (sat) and so forth, whether formed or formless—is without distinction, and because all that exists apart from Brahman does not exist, for name, form, and modification have no existence outside of it, therefore the knowers of Brahman call that Brahman "Truth" (satya). The question previously introduced was "Does it exist or does it not exist?"; regarding the answer to that, it has been stated: "The Self desired, 'May I be many.'"

Having created, according to his will, the effects such as space and so forth—characterized by truth, reality, and so on—and having entered into them, he became manifold by seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing. Therefore, one should understand that this very cause of space and the rest, residing within the effect, deposited in the supreme firmament—the cave of the heart—is perceived through the specific manifestation of its own cognition; thus it is said: "It exists. With reference to this meaning expressed in the Brāhmaṇa, there is this verse, which is a mantra.

Just as in the preceding [sections] there were five mantras revealing the Self consisting of food and so forth, even so there is a mantra that reveals the existence of the Self as the innermost of all, by means of its function.
Thus ends the sixth section.

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. From that, indeed, the existent was born. That made itself by itself; therefore, it is called 'well-made' (*sukṛta*). What is indeed that 'well-made'? It is essence (*rasa*). For only by obtaining essence does one become blissful. For who indeed could inhale, who could exhale, if this bliss did not exist in the ether? He alone causes bliss. For when one finds fearless support in this invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and baseless [reality], then..."

Then he becomes one who has attained fearlessness. For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Brahman], then fear comes upon him; for that very [Brahman] is the source of fear for the one who knows it but does not realize its true nature. On this point there is also this verse:
(TaittU 2.7.1). Thus ends the seventh section. 7.

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (*asad*). By "non-existent," the unmodified Brahman is meant, which is the opposite of the differentiated forms of name and form; it does not mean absolute non-existence, for there can be no birth of existence from non-existence. "This"—the manifest world characterized by specific names and forms—was in the beginning, prior to its production, nothing other than Brahman denoted by the word "non-existent. From that non-existence, existence indeed arose, produced with its specific names and forms clearly distinguished.

Is there any effect distinct from that [Brahman], as a son is distinct from his father? No, he says. That which is denoted by the word "non-existent" (asat) made itself—that is, it made its own self. Because it is so, that Brahman alone is called "well-made" (*sukṛta*), being itself the agent. It is well known in the world that Brahman is the self-acting agent because it is the cause of all. Or, because it made everything by itself through its entire essence, therefore that very Brahman, even in its form as merit (*puṇya*), is called the cause that is "well-made."

In every respect, however, that which is commonly known in the world as "well-done" (*sukṛta*)—the cause for the attainment of results and so forth—is well-established. Whether it be merit (*pu�ṇya*) or something else, that established usage is possible only if there exists an eternal, intelligent cause; therefore, that Brahman exists, because of the common knowledge of "well-done. For this reason also it exists. Why? Because of its being essence (*rasa*). From what [source] does the established fact of Brahman’s being essence arise? To this he says: "That which is indeed well-done, that is indeed essence."

What is called "rasa" (taste/flavor) is well-known in the world as that which causes satisfaction, produces bliss, and consists of the sweet, sour, and so forth. For having obtained—that is, having reached—rasa itself, this person becomes blissful and happy. In the world, that which is non-existent is never seen to be a cause of bliss. Even learned Brahmins who are free from desire and devoid of longing, though lacking external means of pleasure, are seen to be full of bliss as if they had obtained an external rasa; surely, for them, Brahman itself is that rasa. Therefore, that Brahman exists as the cause of their bliss, like a flavorful substance. For this reason also, it exists.

Why? Because activities such as breathing are observed. For this body, while living, breathes out by means of the out-breath (*apāna*) and breathes in by means of the in-breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, movements pertaining to the wind and the sense organs are seen to be brought about by a collection of causes and effects. And such a collection, which functions toward a single purpose, is not possible without a conscious, non-composite entity, because it is never observed otherwise.

Regarding this, he says: "If this bliss were not deposited in the ether, in the supreme space, in the cave [of the heart], who indeed in the world would inhale?—the meaning is, who would perform the function of exhalation? Who would breathe? Who would perform the act of living? Therefore, that Brahman exists; for the sake of which there are the activities of the body, the organs, and the breathing, and by which alone the bliss of the world is produced. Why so? Because this very Supreme Self causes bliss, causes joy, and brings happiness to the world according to its merit."

The meaning is that this very Self, whose nature is bliss, is perceived by living beings as being delimited by ignorance. That Brahman exists for both the knower and the ignorant because it is the cause of fearlessness and fear respectively; for fearlessness arises by taking refuge in a real entity (sadvastu), whereas the cessation of fear is not possible by taking refuge in an unreal entity (asadvastu).

How is it that [Brahman] is the cause of fearlessness? It is said: for when, because of this reason, this practitioner [abides] in this Brahman—characterized by what?—in that which is "invisible" (*adṛśya*). "Visible" (*dṛśya*) means that which is to be seen, namely a modification (*vikāra*), because a modification exists for the purpose of being seen. That which is not visible is "invisible," meaning it is without modification. In this invisible, unmodified, non-objective state, which is "bodiless" (*anātmya*)—meaning without a body—because it is invisible, it is therefore bodiless; because it is bodiless, it is therefore "indefinable" (*anirukta*). For a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) is what is defined.

A specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) is a modification (*vikāra*), and Brahman is without modification, because it is the cause of all modifications. Therefore, it is "indescribable" (*anirukta*). Since this is so, it is "without abode" (*anilayana*); "abode" (*nilayana*) means a nest or a support; that which is not an abode is "without abode," meaning it has no substratum. The meaning of the sentence is: in this very Brahman—which is invisible, bodiless, indescribable, without abode, and distinct from all qualities of effects—one finds fearlessness. The word "fearless" (*abhayam*) is an adverbial modifier, or else it is transformed into another gender as "fearless" (*abhayām*).

He finds—that is, he obtains—his foundation, his stability, and his true self-nature. Then, at that time, because he no longer perceives that cause of fear consisting in the state of being a transmigrator which is created by ignorance, he becomes one who has attained fearlessness. For when he is established in his own essential nature, then he sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and cognizes nothing else. Indeed, fear arises from another toward another; it is not logical for there to be fear of oneself from oneself. Therefore, the Self alone is the cause of fearlessness for the Self.

For Brahmins are seen to be fearless in every respect even when causes for fear exist; yet that would be irrational if Brahman were not the protection from fear. Therefore, because they are seen to possess fearlessness, there exists that Brahman which is the cause of their fearlessness. When does this practitioner become one who has attained fearlessness? When he sees nothing else and does not perceive any internal difference or division within himself, then he has attained fearlessness—this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, because in the state of ignorance this ignorant person perceives—due to ignorance—an object presented by ignorance like a second moon seen by one with ophthalmia, he creates even a slight (*udapi aram*) interval, a gap, a fissure, or a perception of difference within this very Self, which is Brahman. For the perception of difference itself is the cause of separation; the meaning is that he perceives even a slight difference. Then, from that cause, the perception of difference, fear arises for this Self who perceives difference.

Therefore, for the ignorant person, the self itself is the cause of fear for the self. This is what [the text] says: "That very Brahman is indeed the cause of fear for the ignorant one who perceives duality"—that is, for one who perceives duality by thinking, "The Lord is other than me; I am other than He; He is the transmigrating being. For such a person, who perceives a distinction and makes even a slight separation, fear arises regarding that very Brahman known as the Lord. This is so for one who does not contemplate [it] as oneness. Therefore, even though he is called "learned," he is truly ignorant—he who does not perceive the single, undivided reality of the Self.

For fear arises regarding that which is considered subject to annihilation due to the perception of a cause for annihilation; indeed, the cause of annihilation is itself not subject to annihilation. In that case, it is logical that fear—the effect of perceiving that [cause]—should exist toward the cause of annihilation when there is something to be annihilated. Furthermore, the entire world is seen to be possessed of fear. Therefore, from the observation of fear in the world, it is understood that there must certainly exist a cause of fear—a cause of annihilation whose nature is not itself annihilated—from which the world fears. On this point as well, there is this verse: [The verse follows: "Since fear exists, there must be a cause of fear; If there were no cause of fear, how could fear arise? That very thing which causes fear is the cause of fear; Therefore, one should abandon both the fear and its cause. This is the meaning of the verse. It is established that the cause of annihilation is not itself subject to annihilation. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the fact that the world fears annihilation. This concludes the demonstration of the Self's existence through the inference based on the perception of fear. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is established by the inference based on the perception of desire and aversion. For desire and aversion are observed in the world; they are directed toward objects such as pleasure and pain, and they possess a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of desire and aversion is the seeking of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired. Since these two do not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of desire and aversion. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of cognition. For cognition is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as color and sound, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of cognition is the apprehension of objects. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of cognition. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of memory. For memory is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects previously perceived, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of memory is the recollection of what was previously experienced. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of memory. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya). For the notion of "I" is observed in the world; it is directed toward the body, senses, and mind, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the "I-notion" is the conceit of "I. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the "I-notion. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the agent of action. For the agency of action is observed in the world; it is directed toward actions such as walking and sitting, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the agent is the capacity to act. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the agent of action. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the enjoyer of fruit. For the enjoyment of fruit is observed in the world; it is directed toward fruits such as pleasure and pain, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the enjoyer is the capacity to experience. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the enjoyer of fruit. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the controller of the body. For the control of the body is observed in the world; it is directed toward the body, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the controller is the capacity to direct. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the controller of the body. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the witness. For witnessing is observed in the world; it is directed toward the body, senses, mind, and mental states, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the witness is the capacity to observe. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the witness. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the knower. For knowing is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as color and sound, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the knower is the capacity to know. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the knower. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the seer. For seeing is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as color and sound, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the seer is the capacity to see. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the seer. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the hearer. For hearing is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as sound, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the hearer is the capacity to hear. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the hearer. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the smeller. For smelling is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as fragrance, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the smeller is the capacity to smell. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the smeller. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the taster. For tasting is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as taste, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the taster is the capacity to taste. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the taster. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the toucher. For touching is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as touch, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the toucher is the capacity to touch. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the toucher. Furthermore, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the thinker. For thinking is observed in the world; it is directed toward objects such as color and sound, and it possesses a specific nature. Just as the nature of fire is heat, so too the nature of the thinker is the capacity to think. Since this does not exist without a substratum, a substratum must exist. And that substratum is the Self. Thus, the existence of the Self is proven by the inference based on the perception of the thinker.
