"From fear of him the wind blows; from fear of him the sun rises; from fear of him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run forth. This is the inquiry into bliss. Suppose there were a young man, well-versed in the Vedas, most learned, most firm, and most strong; suppose this entire earth were filled with his wealth. That is one unit of human bliss. A hundred such units of human bliss... [are equal to one unit of the bliss of the Gandharvas]. (TaittU 2.8.1)

That, Ānanda, is one unit of bliss among human *gandharvas* and for a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire. A hundred units of bliss of human *gandharvas* constitute one unit of bliss among divine *gandharvas* and for a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire. A hundred units of bliss of divine *gandharvas* constitute one unit of bliss among the ancestors (*pitṛs*) who dwell in the long-lasting world and for a learned *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire.
A hundred units of bliss of those ancestors who dwell in the long-lasting world constitute one unit of bliss among the gods born of themselves (*ājānajā devāḥ*).

And [the bliss] of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who is not overcome by desire; a hundredfold the bliss of those gods born of noble birth (*ājānajāna*) is equal to one bliss of the gods who are deities by action (*karmadeva*), who reach the state of gods through their ritual acts—and also of a learned Vedic scholar who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of those gods who are deities by action is equal to one bliss of the gods—and also of a learned Vedic scholar who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the bliss of those gods is equal to one bliss of Indra.

And that of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. A hundred joys of Indra are equal to one joy of Bṛhaspati, and that of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. A hundred joys of Bṛhaspati are equal to one joy of Prajāpati, and that of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. A hundred joys of Prajāpati are equal to one joy of Brahman, and that of a learned Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.4)

"Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises; out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on. For the wind and the others, though they are themselves powerful lords and highly worthy, proceed with regularity in their tasks of blowing and so forth despite the great effort involved. This is appropriate only if there is a ruler; since their activity proceeds according to a fixed law, there must therefore exist a Brahman as their ruler who is the cause of their fear.

Since those [beings] proceed out of fear of this Brahman like servants of a king, and that cause of fear is bliss (*ānanda*), which is Brahman—there follows this inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*) into that very bliss of Brahman. What is to be inquired about regarding bliss? It is said: Is bliss produced by the connection between an object and a subject, like worldly bliss, or is it intrinsic (*svābhāvika*)? Such is this inquiry into bliss.

In this context, worldly bliss (*laukika-ānanda*) is the most excellent, being characterized by the perfection of external and internal means. It is this very [bliss] that is pointed out for the purpose of following after the bliss of Brahmā (*brahmānanda*). For, by means of this well-known bliss, the bliss that is accessible to a mind whose perception of sense objects has been turned away can be followed after.

Even worldly bliss (*laukika-ānanda*) is merely a portion of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). When consciousness is obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*), and as that ignorance increases, it becomes "worldly"—unstable and fluctuating in the world—being manifested by Brahmā and others through the power of karma, and by virtue of their connection with the means of perception such as objects, in accordance with their respective levels of knowledge.

That very [bliss] is manifested through the removal of ignorance, desire, and karma as the bliss of a learned Śrotriya who is untouched by desire, perceived directly in progressively higher stages beginning with humans and Gandharvas, increasing a hundredfold at each step up to the bliss of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha. However, when the distinction between object and subject created by ignorance is set aside by knowledge, there remains the natural, perfect, one, non-dual bliss; wishing to illustrate this point, the text says: "A youth," meaning one in the first stage of life.

"Sādhuyuvā" means one who is both virtuous (*sādhu*) and young (*yuvā*); this is an adjective qualifying the youth. For even a youth may be unvirtuous, and even one who is not young may be virtuous; therefore, the qualification "virtuous and young" (*sādhuyuvā*) is used. "Adhyāyaka" means one who has studied the Vedas. "Āśiṣṭha" means most skilled in instruction. "Dṛḍhiṣṭha" means most firm. "Baliṣṭha" means strongest. Thus, he is endowed with these internal spiritual means.

This entire vast earth belongs to him, endowed with all wealth—meaning that as a king and lord of the earth, he possesses everything through riches which serve as the means for enjoyment, whether for visible purposes or for invisible purposes as the means for performing ritual acts. And whatever joy he has, that is one human joy—the single, preeminent joy of human beings. A hundred such human joys constitute one joy of the human *gandharvas*. The joy of the human *gandharvas* is a hundred times superior to human joy.

Being human, they have attained the state of a *gandharva* through a particular excellence of karma and knowledge; thus they are human *gandharvas*. For they are endowed with powers such as invisibility and possess subtle bodies and instruments. Therefore, their resistance is slight, and they possess the power to resist the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) as well as the perfection of the means [for such power]. Consequently, for a human *gandharva* who is unimpeded and capable of counteraction, there arises clarity of mind (*cittaprasāda*). From that specific clarity, a specific excellence of happiness is manifested.

Thus, as one proceeds from each preceding stage to each succeeding stage, an excellence of bliss arises that is a hundredfold greater due to the specific excellence of serenity. However, the mention of "one who is not overcome by desire" at the outset is for the purpose of stating that the excellence of bliss—belonging to a learned *śrotriya* who is not struck down by the desire for the enjoyment of human objects—is a hundredfold greater than human bliss and is equal to that of a human *gandharva*. In the phrase "the virtuous youth who has studied," being a *śrotriya* and being free from vice (*avṛjina*) are implied.

For those [pleasures] are indeed indistinct everywhere; however, freedom from being overcome by desire (*akāmahatatva*) is distinguished according to the excellence or inferiority of the objects for the sake of the excellence or inferiority of pleasure. Therefore, there is the mention of "those not overcome by desire," because through its specific gradations, one perceives a hundredfold increase in pleasure, which serves as the means for attaining supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). The rest has been explained. "The celestial Gandharvas" refers to their very birth. "Of those whose world is long-lasting" is an epithet of the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*).

Those ancestors whose world endures for a long time are called *ciralokaloka*. "Ājāna" refers to the world of the gods (*devaloka*); those born in that *ājāna* are the *ājānajā* gods, who are born in divine stations through the excellence of their *smārta* (tradition-based) rituals. The *karma-devas* are those who reach even the status of gods solely through Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*. The "gods" (*deva*) here are the thirty-three *havirbhuj* (sacrificial-eating) deities; Indra is their lord, and Bṛhaspati is his preceptor.

Prajāpati is Virāj, whose body is the three worlds; he is Brahmā, consisting of both the collective and the individual, pervading the entire sphere of transmigratory existence. Therein these various distinctions of bliss attain unity, as do the dharma caused by that, the knowledge concerning it, and the unsurpassed state of being untouched by desire. This is that Hiraṇyagarbha, this Brahmā; his bliss is perceived directly in every way by the learned Śrotriya who is free from crookedness and untouched by desire.

Therefore, it is understood that these three are the means [to the realization of Brahman]. Among them, being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being free from crookedness (*avṛjinatva*) are constant requirements, whereas being unaffected by desire (*akāmahatatva*) is what is preeminent; thus, its status as the most excellent means is understood. And through the excellence of this state of being unaffected by desire, there is perceived the bliss of Brahman directly experienced by the learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), which constitutes but a single fraction of that supreme bliss. This is known from another scriptural passage: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss."

This very bliss is that of which all other portions are like scattered droplets from the waters of the ocean; where they have attained unity, that is this supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because it is natural non-duality (*advaitatva*). Here, there is no distinction between bliss and the one who experiences bliss.

That which is here in a person and that which is yonder in the sun are one. He who knows this, departing from this world, passes into this self consisting of food; he passes into this self consisting of vital breath; he passes into this self consisting of mind; he passes into this self consisting of consciousness; he passes into this self consisting of bliss. On this there is also this verse: Thus ends the eighth Anuvāka. 8.

This result of the inquiry is now summarized: "He who is this person" (sa yaścāyaṃ puruṣaḥ). He who is hidden in the cave, having created the effects beginning with space and ending with that which consists of food (*annamaya*), and having entered into that very [creation], is pointed out by the words "he who. Who is he? This person within the body.

That which is in the sun—that supreme bliss which is directly perceived by one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), of which Brahmā and other beings worthy of happiness partake as a single portion—is indicated by the words "that which is in the sun. It is one, just like the oneness of space within a jar situated in a different location. Now, an objection may be raised: when that [bliss] is being indicated, the internal description "that which is this in the person" is not appropriate without qualification, whereas the description "that which is in the right eye" would be appropriate because of its well-known familiarity. To this we say: no.

Because of the context of the Supreme. For it is the Supreme Self that has been introduced here—as in "In the unseen, the bodiless, out of fear of Him the wind blows," and "This is the inquiry into bliss. Indeed, it is not proper to mention something that is neither the subject at hand nor relevant without cause; moreover, the knowledge of the Supreme Self is what is intended to be taught. Therefore, it is the Supreme alone who is indicated by the words "He is one. [Objection: But the inquiry into bliss was the subject at hand; its result must also be concluded.

Inseparable, intrinsic bliss is the Supreme Self alone; it is not produced by the relationship between an object and a subject. But is this not a description precisely suited to that [bliss], namely: "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun, these are one," where the distinction residing in different loci is sublated? Even so, would not the mention of the specific quality of the sun be purposeless? It is not purposeless, for it serves to eliminate [the notions of] superiority and inferiority.

For if that which is the supreme excellence of duality—characterized by the formed and the formless—which resides within the sun, becomes equal to the supreme bliss upon the dissolution of the distinctions pertaining to the person, then for one who has attained that state there is neither any superiority nor inferiority; thus it is logical that he "finds fearless support. The subsequent question regarding "it exists" and "it does not exist" has been explained.

Because of [the evidence of] activity, the attainment of the essence of things, life, fearlessness, support, the perception of fear, and logical possibility, that cause of space and so forth—Brahman—truly exists; thus, one preliminary question has been resolved. There remain two other preliminary questions concerning the attainment and non-attainment of Brahman by the knower and the ignorant respectively. Among these, the final preliminary question is whether the knower attains [Brahman] or does not attain it. To resolve that, [the following] is stated. Since the middle preliminary question is resolved by the very resolution of the final one, no further effort is made to resolve it.

Whoever knows thus—having abandoned that aforementioned Brahman along with its distinctions of superiority and inferiority, knowing "I am non-dual, truth, knowledge, and infinite"—is an "evamvit" (one who knows thus). This is because the word "thus" (evam) has the sense of referring back to what has been previously mentioned.

What is that? Having departed from this world—this world being a collection of perceived and unperceived desired objects—he, having departed from this world and turned back, becoming indifferent, enters into this self consisting of food as previously explained; he does not perceive the multitude of objects as distinct from the body-self consisting of food, but rather perceives everything that has become gross as the self consisting of food; such is the meaning.

Then he approaches this inner one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), which resides within the self consisting of food (*annamaya*) and is undivided; then he approaches this self consisting of mind (*manomaya*), this self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and this self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Then he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, non-self, indefinable, and without abode. Regarding this, it must be considered: who is this knower of suchness, and how does he transition? Is the agent of the transition distinct from the supreme Self, or is it that very Self?

What follows from this? If it were another [than Brahman], there would be a contradiction with the Śruti: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing"; "He does not know, thinking, 'He is one and I am another'; and "That thou art, the One alone without a second. On the other hand, if it is He Himself who approaches the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), then the relationship of object and agent is untenable; furthermore, either the Supreme Lord Himself would be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), or the Supreme would be non-existent. If the fault incurred in either case cannot be avoided, then this inquiry is useless.

Now, if a fault does not apply to one of the two positions, or if the third position is faultless, then that alone would be the meaning of the treatise, and the inquiry would be useless. This is not so, because the purpose is to determine that [faultless position]. It is true that if a fault were encountered and could not be avoided, then once one of the two or the third position were determined to be faultless, the inquiry would indeed be useless; but since that has not been determined, this inquiry is meaningful for the sake of such determination. Truly, the inquiry is meaningful.

[The opponent asks: "Is it because you intend to determine the meaning of the scripture that you reflect, yet will not reach a conclusion? Is there some Vedic statement that ought not to be determined? [The teacher replies: "No. Rather, it is because there are many adversaries. You are a proponent of unity (*ekatvavādī*), for you are singular in your devotion to the meaning of the Veda. There are indeed many proponents of diversity (*nānātvavādinaḥ*) who are outside the Veda; as for where their opposition lies, I have this doubt: 'Will you not resolve it? This very thing is my blessing—that you address me, a single yogi, as having many yogis as your adversaries."

Therefore, I shall conquer all; I undertake this reflection. But that [Self] alone would be [the object], because it is that state which is intended to be expressed here. For by the knowledge of That, the state of the Supreme Self is what is intended to be expressed in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Indeed, the attainment of the nature of one thing by another is not logically possible. [Objection: But even for him (the individual soul), the attainment of that state is equally impossible. [Reply: No, because its purpose is the removal of the non-Self created by ignorance.

For that attainment of one's own Self which is taught through the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) has as its purpose the removal of the non-Self—which is superimposed as the Self upon the specific objects such as food and so forth, and is produced by ignorance. How is it understood that this is its purpose? From the fact that only knowledge is taught. And the observed effect of knowledge is the cessation of ignorance; therefore, in this case, only knowledge is taught as the means for attaining the Self. If it is argued that it is like the teaching of the knowledge of a path, [we reply: that teaching of knowledge alone as the means does not constitute a reason for [the Self] being that [path]. Why?

If it is argued that [the knowledge of Brahman is not the means], because we observe the instruction of knowledge regarding the path for the sake of reaching another place—for one does not go to a village by means of the village itself—the answer is no, because of the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*). For in that case, knowledge concerning the village is not what is taught; rather, it is knowledge concerning the path to reach it that is taught. It is not so here, where knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman concerning some other means is taught. If it is argued that the knowledge of Brahman, depending on previously mentioned means such as ritual action (*karman*), is taught as the means for attaining the Supreme, we say no.

This has already been refuted by the statement beginning with "Because liberation is eternal," and so forth. Furthermore, the Śruti, in the passage "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," shows that the effect has that [Brahman] as its self. Moreover, the attainment of fearlessness and a firm foundation is logical; for if the one possessed of knowledge perceives nothing other than his own Self, then he finds a fearless foundation because there is no other, distinct entity that could be a cause of fear. And since any such other would be a product of ignorance, it is logical that its unreality is perceived through knowledge.

For that non-existence of a second moon is not perceived by one whose eyes are clear and free from cataracts. If it is argued that it is not the case that it is not perceived, we say no; for it is not perceived by those who are in deep sleep or in meditative absorption (*samāhita*). If it is argued that its non-perception in deep sleep is like [non-perception] when one is distracted elsewhere, we say no; because there is a total lack of perception [of all objects]. If it is argued that since something else is perceived during waking and dreaming, [the second moon] must indeed exist, we say no; for waking and dreaming are produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The perception of something other [than the Self] during waking and dreaming is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is absent when there is knowledge (*vidyā*). If it is argued that even the non-perception [of objects] in deep sleep is produced by ignorance, we say no; for it is innate. Indeed, the true nature (*tattva*) of a substance is its changelessness, because it is independent of anything else. Change is not the true nature, because it is dependent on another. For the true nature of a thing does not depend on causal factors (*kāraka*); rather, it is a particularity (*viśeṣa*) that depends on causal factors, and a particularity is a modification (*vikriyā*). And in waking and dreaming, perception is such a particularity.

For that which has a nature independent of anything else is its true reality (*tattva*); that which depends on another is not its true reality, because it would cease to exist in the absence of that other. Therefore, because it is inherent, there is no distinction in deep sleep as there is in the waking and dreaming states. However, for those who hold that God is other than the Self and that the effect is other [than the cause], fear does not cease; for fear has another as its cause, and it is impossible for an existing thing to perish or for a non-existing thing to come into being. Nor can a non-existent thing attain selfhood.

If it is argued that something else which is dependent [on another] can be a cause of fear, we say no; for that case is equal [to the first]. Whatever other cause of fear there might be—whether eternal or non-eternal—that depends upon a concomitant factor such as *dharma* and so forth, for that too, because there is no destruction of its own self (*ātman*), fear would not cease. Or, if there were destruction of the self, then since existence and non-existence would result in one becoming the other, there would be a total lack of confidence in everything. However, in the view of unity (*ekatva*), there is no fault, because the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) along with its causes is merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).

For the second moon seen by one suffering from ophthalmia (timira) has neither origination nor destruction. If it is argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) possess that same nature [of being unreal], we say no, because they are perceived directly. Discrimination (*viveka*) and non-discrimination (*aviveka*) are perceived as residing within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), just like color-form (*rūpa*) and other objects; for a color-form, while being directly perceived, does not have the status of being a property of the seer. Furthermore, ignorance is manifested through one's own experience in the form: "I am deluded," "my consciousness is undiscriminating. Likewise, the discrimination of knowledge is experienced.

The wise teach their own knowledge to others, and others likewise comprehend it. Therefore, knowledge and ignorance belong to the side of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form themselves do not constitute the attributes of the Self (*ātman*). This is because of another scriptural passage: "That which is distinct from these two, name-and-form, and that which lies between them—that is Brahman. Furthermore, those two, name-and-form, are merely conceptualized like day and night in relation to the sun; they do not exist in an ultimate sense.

If it is argued that because there is no difference [between the self and Brahman], the attainment of this self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is untenable due to the impossibility of there being both an object and an agent of action, we say: no; for this "attainment" is merely a matter of cognition (*vijñānamātra*). Here, an actual physical transition like that of a leech is not taught; rather, the meaning of the scriptural term "attainment" is simply cognition. If it is asked, "But surely a literal attainment is heard in the text, as in the phrase 'he attains' (*upasaṅkramati*)," we reply: no; because such a literal transition is not observed in the case of the self consisting of food (*annamaya*).

For no transition, whether like that of a leech or otherwise, is observed for one who approaches the *annamaya* [self] from this external world. If it is argued that the transition to the self occurs through the return of the *manomaya* or the *vijñānamaya* after they have gone outwards, we say no; because of the contradiction of action upon oneself. For, while the context states that "one approaches another, the *annamaya*," it would be a contradiction if the *manomaya* or the *vijñānamaya* were to approach its own very self.

Likewise, the transition of the self into that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya) is not tenable. Therefore, "transition" is neither an attainment, nor does it consist in one of the sheaths beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) acting as the agent; rather, by process of elimination, it is established that transition is merely a cognition whose agent is distinct from the selves beginning with the one consisting of food and ending with the one consisting of bliss.

If it is pure consciousness alone, then for that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which dwells within all and is the innermost of all, having created the entire effect beginning with space and ending with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), and having entered therein, there arises the delusion of selfhood regarding the non-self—such as the body consisting of food—due to its connection with the cave of the heart. This delusion perishes through the process of "transition" (*saṅkramaṇa*), by means of the arising of discriminative knowledge of the Self. It is in this destruction of the delusion caused by ignorance that the word "transition" is used figuratively; for otherwise, a transition of the omnipresent Self is not possible, and because there is no other entity [into which it could move].

Nor is there a transition of the self into itself; for a leech does not transition into its own self. Therefore, for the sake of realizing the Self characterized as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," such things as becoming many, creation, entering, obtaining the essence, fearlessness, and transition are merely conceptualized within Brahman, which is the object of all worldly discourse. However, in the ultimate sense, no conceptual construction whatsoever is possible in Brahman, which is free from all differentiation.

Having approached this very Self, which is free from conceptual construction, in this manner and having known it, one does not fear anything; one finds the foundation of fearlessness. With regard to this meaning, there is also this verse. This mantra serves to briefly illuminate the entire subject matter of this section, the meaning of the *Ānandavallī*. Thus ends the eighth section (*anu-vāka*).

(TaittUBh_2,1.5) "From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—having known that bliss of Brahman, one does not fear anything from anywhere. Indeed, this [knowledge] does not cause him to regret: "Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil? He who knows thus protects these two by means of the Self; for he who knows thus protects both by means of the Self. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. (TaittU_2,9.1) Thus ends the ninth section. // 9 //
Thus ends the Brahmavallī.

Because from that non-conceptual Self—which possesses the aforementioned characteristics and consists of non-dual bliss—the various words (vācaḥ), which are designations having as their objects things with conceptual attributes such as substance and so forth, are employed by speakers for the purpose of illumination even regarding Brahman, who is non-conceptual and non-dual; yet, failing to reach and failing to illuminate [Him], they turn back and are withdrawn by their own inherent power. "Mind" (manaḥ) refers to the cognition (vijñāna).

And that designation which has been set in motion with respect to an object—even one beyond the senses—proceeds toward that very object for the purpose of illumination; and wherever there is cognition, there the activity of speech occurs. Therefore, in all cases, the activity of both speech and mind, as well as their respective designations and cognitions, proceeds simultaneously.

Therefore, since even words employed in every possible way by speakers to reveal Brahman turn back—along with the mind and the consciousness capable of illuminating everything—from that which is beyond the scope of cognition, inexpressible, and characterized by such attributes as being invisible, that bliss of Brahman belongs to the one learned in the Vedas, free from crookedness, untouched by desire, liberated from all longings, who has become the Self; it is natural, eternal, undivided, the supreme bliss, free from the relationship between object and subject.

The knower of Brahman, according to the method described, fears nothing from any source, because of the absence of a cause [for fear]. For there exists no other distinct entity apart from that Knower from which he might fear. It is logical that fear arises for one who creates an internal separation through ignorance, according to the teaching: "Then fear comes to him. But for the Knower, since the effects of ignorance—like a second moon seen by one with a cataract—have been destroyed, it is fitting that he "fears nothing from any source," as the cause of fear no longer exists.

The mantra is cited as being "consisting of mind" because the mind is the means for the realization of Brahman. In that context, having superimposed the nature of Brahman [upon the mind], the mere prohibition of fear is stated in the form "he fears nothing at any time" for the purpose of praising it. Here, however, in the context of non-duality, the very cause of fear is prohibited by the statement "he does not fear from anything whatsoever."

"Now, surely there exists a cause for fear: the non-performance of good and the performance of evil. Not so. How is this said?—"This," meaning that which has been described as such; "ha vāva" are used for emphasis. It does not burn, does not agitate, and does not torment. But how is it said that the non-performance of good and the performance of evil do not burn? Because at the time when death is near, there arises remorse [thinking]: "Why, for what reason, did I not perform, did I not do, good and auspicious action?"

Likewise, there arises remorse due to the fear of suffering such as falling into hell, thinking, "Why have I committed this forbidden evil deed? I have indeed done it. These two—the failure to perform what is good and the performance of what is evil—do not afflict him in the same way that they afflict the ignorant man.

Why, then, do they not afflict the man of knowledge? It is said: he who knows thus protects—that is, pleases or strengthens—himself by realizing that these two, the good and the evil, are the causes of affliction; the meaning is that he perceives both through the state of the Supreme Self. For since this knower does so, having rendered both merit and demerit empty of their own specific forms by means of the very form of the Self, he indeed protects himself.

Who? He who knows thus—that is, he who knows the non-dual blissful Brahman as described—his merit and demerit, being seen as his own self-nature, become powerless and no longer cause torment by initiating another birth. Thus, this very Brahma-vidyā Upaniṣad, as explained in this Vallī, has revealed the supreme secret among all sciences; the meaning is that the highest good is seated within it.

The Bhṛgu Vally: Om. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be full of splendor; may we never harbor enmity toward one another. Om. Peace! Peace! Peace!

Brahman—truth, knowledge, infinite—having created the effects beginning with space and ending with that which consists of food (the physical body), entered into them; because it is perceived as if possessing distinctions [within those effects], one should realize: "I am that very Bliss," which is distinct from all effects and possesses attributes such as being invisible. This is because the purpose of the entry was for that very end. For one who realizes this, good and evil actions do not become the initiators of future births; such is the intended meaning of the Ānandavallī.

The knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) has been completed. Hereafter, austerity (tapas), which is the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman, must be described; furthermore, meditations (upāsanā) concerning food and other subjects have not yet been stated. Therefore, this [section] is commenced.

The narrative is for the purpose of praising knowledge; it was spoken by a father to his beloved son, as in the case of Bhṛgu Vāruṇi. The word "vai" is a reminder of what is well-known; the one well-known by the name Bhṛgu is thus reminded. Vāruṇi is the offspring of Varuṇa; desiring to know Brahman, he approached his father Varuṇa with this mantra: "Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman. [The meaning is: "Teach," that is, instruct or explain.

And that father, having spoken these words to his son who had approached him according to the prescribed rule—namely, "Food, breath, eye, ear, mind, and speech"—explained that food is the body and breath is its internal consumer; immediately thereafter, he stated that the eye, ear, mind, and speech are the instruments of perception, serving as the gateways for the realization of Brahman. Having thus described these gateways, beginning with food, he spoke to Bhrigu regarding the definition of Brahman. What was that?

Since from this [Brahman] these beings, beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass, are born; since by it, once born, they live—that is, they sustain their vital breaths—and grow; and at the time of destruction, toward which they go—that is, they return to that Brahman and enter into identity with it—such that throughout the times of origin, subsistence, and dissolution, the beings do not abandon their nature as that [Brahman]: this is the defining characteristic of Brahman. Therefore, desire to know that Brahman; seek to know it in its specific detail.

The meaning is: "Understand that Brahman which has such characteristics by means of food and so forth. And another Śruti passage—*prāṇasya prāṇam uta cakṣuṣaścakṣur uta śrotrasya śrotram annasyānnam manaso ye mano viduste nicikyurbrahma purāṇam agryam* ("Those who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of mind—they have perceived the ancient, foremost Brahman")—shows that these are the doors for the realization of Brahman.

Having heard from his father the gateways for the attainment of Brahman and the definition of Brahman, that Bhṛgu performed austerity—that is, he practiced it—as the means for the attainment of Brahman. But how did Bhṛgu come to understand that austerity was the means, even though it had not been explicitly taught? It was because [the teaching] was incomplete; for when explaining the gateways and the definition for the realization of Brahman through food and so forth, the father stated, "From which indeed these... and so on. That [teaching] was indeed incomplete, because Brahman itself had not been directly pointed out.

For otherwise, he would have pointed out Brahman by its very nature to his son who desired to know it, saying, "Brahman is of such-and-such a form. But he did not point it out in that way; rather, he spoke with something still remaining. Therefore, it is understood that the father certainly expects some other means for the realization of Brahman. And the practice of specific austerity is [the means] because it is the most effective of all.

For it is well known in the world that among all means of accomplishment whose objects are fixed to be achieved, austerity (*tapas*) alone is the most effective means. Therefore, even though it was not specifically instructed by his father, Bhṛgu undertook austerity as a means for the realization of Brahman. And that austerity consists in the concentration of the external and internal organs, because the realization of Brahman occurs through its medium. For the Smṛti says: "The one-pointedness of the mind and the senses is the supreme austerity; it is superior to all duties, and it is declared to be the highest duty. Having performed that austerity, he [Bhṛgu]—1.

"Food is Brahman," he understood. "Verily, from food alone these beings are born; once born, they live by food; into food they pass and merge. Having realized this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity (*tapas*); austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity—thus ends the second section. (TaittUBh_3,2.1) // 2 //

"He understood—that is, he realized—'Food is Brahman. For that [food] indeed possesses the characteristics previously described. How so? 'For truly, from food alone these beings are born; by food, once born, they live; into food they enter at death and merge. Therefore, the intention is that it is logical for food to be Brahman. Having thus performed austerity and having realized that 'Food is Brahman,' both through its defining characteristics and through logical reasoning, he again fell into doubt and approached his father Varuṇa."

"Teach me, O Venerable One, about Brahman. What, then, is the cause of his doubt? It is said: because he observes that food has an origin. Furthermore, the repeated instruction regarding austerity (*tapas*) is for the purpose of determining it to be the most excellent means. As long as the defining characteristic of Brahman—which is unsurpassed—has not been realized, and as long as the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) does not cease, so long is austerity alone your means. The meaning is: "By austerity alone, seek to understand Brahman. The rest is straightforward.

"Breath is Brahman," he understood. "Indeed, from breath alone these beings are born; by breath, once born, they live; into breath they enter at their passing. Having realized this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity—(TaittU 3.3.1). Thus ends the third section. 3.

"Consciousness is Brahman," he understood. "For indeed, from consciousness alone these beings are born; by consciousness, once born, they live; into consciousness they enter at their passing. Having understood this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. He said to him, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity—(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.5.1). Thus ends the fifth section.

"Bliss is Brahman," so he understood. Indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; into bliss they enter at their passing away. This is that knowledge of Bhārgava Vāruṇi, established in the highest heaven. He who knows this becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa); he becomes great in fame. Thus ends the sixth section.

Thus, having purified his self through austerity (tapas) and perceiving the characteristics of Brahman completely within the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, Bhṛgu gradually entered further inward and came to know Brahman as the innermost bliss through austerity alone as the means. Therefore, the meaning of this section is that one who desires to know Brahman must practice supreme austerity, characterized by the concentration of both the external and internal organs.

Now, having concluded the narrative, the Śruti states in its own words the purpose accomplished by that narrative: "This very Vāruṇī knowledge—known by Bhṛgu as the Bhārgavī, taught by Varuṇa—is established and fully perfected in the supreme non-dual bliss within the cave of the heart-ether, having proceeded forth from the Self consisting of food."

Whoever else, by this very means of austerity and by this same sequence, enters thus and knows Brahman as bliss—he, being established through that knowledge, becomes firmly established in bliss, the supreme Brahman; the meaning is that he becomes Brahman itself. And the visible fruit for him is stated: "Possessed of food" (*annavān*) means that abundant food exists for him. For if it were merely a matter of existence, everyone would indeed be "possessed of food," and there would be no distinction for the knowledge.

The meaning is that by eating thus, one becomes an "eater of food" (annāda) with a kindled digestive fire. One becomes great. By what means is this greatness attained? To this he says: by progeny, such as sons and so forth; by cattle, such as cows, horses, and so forth; and by Brahman-splendor (brahmavarcasa), which is the luster resulting from tranquility, self-control, knowledge, and the like. One becomes great through fame (kīrti), that is, renown caused by virtuous conduct.

"One should not revile food; that is his vow. Breath, indeed, is food; the body is the eater of food. The body is established in breath; breath is established in the body. Thus, this food is established in food. He who knows this food as established in food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food, an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. Thus ends the seventh section. (TaittUBh_3.3–6) (TaittU_3.7.1)

Furthermore, since Brahman is known through food acting as a gateway, one should not revile food as one would a teacher; this is the vow prescribed for such a knower of Brahman. This instruction regarding the vow is for the purpose of praising food, and food is worthy of praise because it is the means for the realization of Brahman. Indeed, breath (*prāṇa*) is food, because breath exists within the body. Whatever is established within one's own [body] becomes one's food.

And the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established in the body; therefore, the vital breath is food (*anna*) and the body is the eater of food (*annāda*). Likewise, the body is also food and the vital breath is the eater of food. Why is the body established in the vital breath? Because the stability of the body is caused by it. Therefore, both of these—the body and the vital breath—are food and the eater of food. That by which one is established in the other is food; that by which one provides the establishment for the other is the eater of food.

Therefore, both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body are food and the eater of food. He who thus knows this food as established in food becomes established by means of the very self that is food and the eater of food; moreover, he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food, and so forth, as before.

"One should not reject food; that is his vow. Water, indeed, is food; light is the eater of food. Light is established in water; water is established in light. Thus, this food is established in food. He who knows that this food is established in food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food, an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. Thus ends the eighth section. 8.

"One should not reject food" means one should not avoid it; that vow is for the sake of praise, as before. Thus, food that is not abandoned through the conceptualization of "pure" or "impure" would be praised and magnified. In this manner, one should apply what has been stated to the subsequent cases as well, such as "water, indeed, is food," and so forth.

"One should prepare much food; that is his vow. Earth, indeed, is food; space is the eater of food. Space is established upon the earth; the earth is established upon space. Thus, this food is established upon food. He who knows this food to be established upon food becomes firmly established. He becomes possessed of food, an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. Thus ends the ninth section. 9.
With the mantra "In the waters is light," there is the vow of providing abundant food for the practitioner who meditates upon water and light as having the qualities of food and the eater of food.

"One should not refuse anyone seeking lodging; that is his vow. Therefore, by whatever means possible, he should obtain abundant food. They say, 'Food has been prepared for him. Indeed, this is food prepared at the beginning; food is prepared for him from the beginning. Indeed, this is food prepared in the middle; food is prepared for him from the middle. Indeed, this is food prepared at the end; food is prepared for him from the end. (TaittU 3.10.1) "One should not refuse anyone seeking lodging; that is his vow. Therefore, by whatever means possible, he should obtain abundant food. They say, 'Food has been prepared for him. Indeed, this is food prepared at the beginning; food is prepared for him from the beginning. Indeed, this is food prepared in the middle; food is prepared for him from the middle. Indeed, this is food prepared at the end; food is prepared for him from the end."

Likewise, for one who worships the earth and space, no one at all should refuse him lodging; the meaning is that he should not turn away anyone who has come for the purpose of a dwelling. And when lodging is given, food must indeed be provided. Therefore, by whatever means and in whatever manner possible, he should obtain abundant food; the meaning is that he should make a collection of much food.

Because learned men who possess food, when approached by one seeking food, say "It has been prepared; we have food," and do not refuse him by saying "There is none," for that reason he shall obtain abundant food—this is the connection with what precedes. Furthermore, the greatness of giving food is stated: at whatever time one bestows food, at that very same time it returns to him.

To the question "How so?", this is said: "This food, indeed, prepared with honor and presented to one who has arrived seeking food, in the mouth—that is, in the primary [period of] life, or by the primary mode of conduct"—this is the completion of the sentence. What would be the fruit of that? It is said: "In the mouth—that is, in the earlier period of life, or by the primary mode of conduct—food is prepared for this giver of food; the meaning is that it remains present to him just as it was given."

In this way, in the middle of life and at the middle stage, with middling service; likewise, at the end of life and in the final stage, with inferior service and contempt—in this very manner, food becomes successful and well-digested for him.

"Security" is in speech; "acquisition and security" is in the out-breath and in-breath; "action" is in the hands; "motion" is in the feet; "liberation" is in the anus—these are the human designations. Now, the divine ones: "satisfaction" is in rain; "strength" is in lightning.

Whoever knows this—meaning whoever knows the greatness of food as described above, as well as the fruit of its giving—the aforementioned fruit accrues to him. Now, the method of meditating upon Brahman is stated: "Security (kṣema) in speech. Security means the protection of what has already been acquired. One should meditate thus: "Brahman is established in speech in the form of security. "Acquisition and security (yogakṣema)"—acquisition (yoga) is the obtaining of what has not yet been obtained.

For although those two, acquisition (*yoga*) and preservation (*kṣema*), exist when the *prāṇa* and *apāna* are present, they do not have the *prāṇa* and *apāna* alone as their cause; rather, they have Brahman as their cause. Therefore, Brahman is to be meditated upon as being established in the *prāṇa* and *apāna* in the form of acquisition and preservation. In this same way, among the other [limbs] that follow, Brahman alone is to be meditated upon through its respective forms. Since action is brought about by Brahman, Brahman is to be meditated upon as being established in the hands in the form of action. "Motion" (*gati*) refers to the feet.

"Liberation" refers to the anus. These are the human designations—those pertaining to humans among men; "designations" (samājñā) means internal cognitions, which is to say, knowledges, specific consciousnesses, and objects of meditation. Immediately after that, the divine designations—those pertaining to the gods among the gods—are stated. "Satisfaction" refers to rain; since rain is the cause of satisfaction by way of food and so forth, Brahman itself, established in the form of rain as the essence of satisfaction, is to be meditated upon. Likewise, in other things, Brahman alone is to be meditated upon in its respective forms. Similarly, it is to be meditated upon in lightning in the form of power.

"Glory"—this is with regard to cattle; "light"—this is with regard to the stars; "progeny, immortality, and bliss"—this is with regard to the organ of generation; "the All"—this is with regard to space. One should meditate upon it as the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). One becomes possessed of a foundation. One should meditate upon it as greatness (*mahaḥ*). One becomes great. One should meditate upon it as mind (*manas*). One becomes possessed of mind. (TaittU 3.10.3)

In the form of fame among cattle; in the form of light among the stars; procreation, immortality—the attainment of immortality—and bliss through the son as the means of liberation from debt: all this, which has the generative organ (*upastha*) as its sign, is Brahman alone, established in the generative organ by means of this self; thus it is to be meditated upon. For everything is established in space (*ākāśa*); therefore, that which is everything in space is Brahman alone—it is to be meditated upon. And that space is Brahman itself. Therefore, one should meditate upon it as the foundation of all.

By meditating on [Brahman] as "Foundation" (pratiṣṭhā), one becomes possessed of a foundation. In this same way, regarding the preceding [attributes] as well, it should be understood that whatever fruit is taught in connection with a particular attribute, one becomes possessed of that very thing by meditating on Brahman as such. This is also known from another scriptural passage: "In whatever manner they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become. One should meditate on it as "Greatness" (mahaḥ). "Greatness" means possessing the quality of greatness; by meditating on it thus, one becomes great. One should meditate on it as "Mind" (manas). "Mind" is the act of thinking (manana); by meditating on it thus, one becomes possessed of mind—that is, one becomes capable of reflection.

One should meditate upon that as "the Name" (*nāma*); desires bow down to him. One should meditate upon that as "Brahman"; he becomes possessed of Brahman. One should meditate upon that as "the complete death of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ parimara*); those who hate him, his rivals, and those enemies who are disliked, die around him. That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun—that is one.

One should meditate upon it as "the Name. "Namaḥ" means bowing; one should meditate upon it as possessing the quality of being bowed to. Desires—meaning objects of enjoyment that are desired—bow down, that is, become humble, before this worshiper. One should meditate upon it as "Brahman. One should meditate upon it as the most exalted. One becomes possessed of Brahman, that is, endowed with its qualities. One should meditate upon it as "the complete passing away of Brahman."

The "complete dying around" (*parimara*) of Brahman is that in which five deities—namely lightning, rain, the moon, the sun, and fire—die away. Therefore, Vāyu is the *parimara*, as is well known from another scriptural passage. Since this very Vāyu is non-different from space (*ākāśa*), space is the *parimara* of Brahman. Consequently, one should meditate upon space, whose nature is Vāyu, as the *parimara* of Brahman.

Those who rival this one who knows thus—whether they be hostile enemies or even those who are not hostile—are distinguished as "hostile rivals" (*dviṣantaḥ sapatnāḥ*) because they exist as such. Those hostile rivals perish; they abandon their vital breaths. Furthermore, those who are his unpleasant kinsmen (*bhrātṛvya*), even if they are not hostile, they too perish. Beginning with the statement that "breath is indeed food and the body is the eater of food," it has been explained that the relationship of food and eater belongs only to the effects, ending with space.

Granted that this has been said; what follows from it? This is established: transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists in the state of being the eater and the eaten, pertains only to the realm of effects, and not to the Self (*ātman*). However, it is figuratively attributed to the Self through delusion. [Objection: But surely the individual self (*ātman*) is also an effect of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); therefore, transmigratory existence is logically applicable to it. [Reply: No, because of the scriptural teaching regarding the entry of that which is itself non-transmigratory. For in the passage, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (*tatsṛṣṭvā tad evānuprāviśat*), the entry into the effects by the Supreme Self—the cause of ether and the rest—is heard to belong precisely to that which is non-transmigratory.

Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*), which has entered into the effect, is indeed the Supreme Self, free from transmigratory existence; for it is logical that the same agent is implied by the expression "having created, he entered. Furthermore, if the agent of the two actions of creation and entering is one and the same, then the use of the suffix *-ktvā* is appropriate. If it is argued that for one who has entered, there must be the attainment of a different state of being, we say no; for that objection regarding the entry having a different purpose has already been refuted. And if it is argued that because of the specific scriptural qualification "by this living self," the entry must be into something possessing different attributes, we say no.

The statement "That thou art" expresses that very state [of being Brahman]. If it is argued that this identification (*sampad*) is for the purpose of negating that [state] in one who has already attained another state, we say no; because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That thou art. If it is argued that the transmigratory nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is observed, we say no; because the perceiver cannot itself be perceived. If it is argued that the Self is perceived as qualified by the attributes of transmigratory existence, we say no; because qualities are not distinct from the possessor of those qualities, it is impossible for the Self to be an object of action.

If it is argued that, just as heat and light cannot logically be the objects of burning or illumination, so too suffering and the like are inferred from the observation of fear and so forth [in the Self], we say: no. Since fear and suffering are themselves perceived, they cannot be attributes of the perceiver. If it is argued that this contradicts the systems of logic such as those of the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika, we say: no. For those systems are established as erroneous due to their lack of a valid foundation and their contradiction with the Veda. Furthermore, the non-transmigratory nature of the Self is established by both scripture and reasoning, as well as by its oneness.
How is oneness expressed? "He who is here in the person and he who is there in the sun are one"—thus everything is as previously stated.

He who knows thus, having departed from this world, having reached this self consisting of food, having reached this self consisting of vital breath, having reached this self consisting of mind, having reached this self consisting of consciousness, having reached this self consisting of bliss, wandering through these worlds at will and assuming forms at will, sits singing this Sāman: "Hā3vu! Hā3vu! Hā3vu! (TaittU 3.10.5)

Having ascended through the sequence beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) up to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), he remains singing that *sāman*. The meaning of the verse "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) has been explained in detail by the *Ānandavallī*, which serves as its commentary. However, the expansion of the meaning of the statement regarding its fruit—"He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman"—has not yet been stated.

It must now be explained who these desires are, what their objects are, and how one partakes together with Brahman; this is what is commenced here. In that regard, within the narrative of the father and son which serves as a supplement to the preceding knowledge, austerity has been declared to be the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman. Furthermore, the application of all effects—from the vital breaths up to ether—as food and the eater of food has been stated, as have the meditations concerning Brahman.

Furthermore, all desires have been shown to be accomplished by various specific means and to consist of distinct objects such as space and the like. However, if [Brahman] were a single unity, the fulfillment of desires according to one's wish would be impossible, because everything born of differentiation would be identical with its own Self. In that case, how is it said that "one who knows thus enjoys all desires simultaneously through the nature of Brahman"? It is because of the logical possibility of being the Self of all.

To explain how the realization of being the Self of all is established, he says: by means of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self residing in the Sun and the Person, one discards the notions of superiority and inferiority; having successively passed through the selves beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*)—which are imagined through ignorance and culminating in the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*)—one attains the fruit that is the ultimate goal: Brahman, which is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite, characterized by attributes such as being invisible, natural bliss, unborn, immortal, fearless, and non-dual. The connection with the distant [verb] is: "wandering through these worlds," namely the earth and so forth. How does one wander?

"Kāmānnī" means one for whom food comes from desire; likewise, "kāmarūpī" means one who assumes forms at will. Wandering through these worlds with his entire self, experiencing them as his own self, he remains sitting while singing this Sāman. Because of its equality, Brahman itself is the Sāman; singing—that is, sounding—it in a form non-different from all things, he proclaims the oneness of the Self. For the sake of favoring the world, he remains sitting, singing the fruit of that realization: the state of having achieved the ultimate goal, namely, "Hā āvu, hā āvu, hā āvu. (Hā āvu expresses wonder.)
The word "aho" is used here in this sense to express the utmost amazement. // 5 //

(I am food, I am food, I am food. I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food. I am the maker of *śloka*, I am the maker of *śloka*, I am the maker of *śloka*. I am the first-born of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), prior even to the gods, at the navel of immortality. He who gives me, he indeed protects me. I eat the food that eats food. I have surpassed the entire world. The light of heaven! He who knows thus—this is the Upaniṣad. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 3.10.5–6)
Thus ends the tenth section. Thus ends the Bhṛguvallī. Thus ends the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.

What, then, is this wonder? It is said: although the Self is non-dual and stainless (*nirañjana*), I am indeed both the food and the eater of food. Furthermore, I alone am the maker of the *śloka*. A *śloka* is the aggregate of food and the eater of food; its maker is the conscious one. Or rather, I have fashioned this aggregate by means of its being for the sake of another—since food itself exists for the sake of the eater, who is manifold in nature—and on account of that dependence upon another. The triple repetition is for the purpose of manifesting the sense of wonder. "I am" (*asmi*) means "I exist."

The "first-born" (*prathamaja*) is one born first, arisen at the beginning. Of this world of truth (*ṛta*), consisting of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), he is the navel of immortality (*amṛta*) even prior to the gods; that is to say, immortality centered in me is the navel, or the middle, for living beings. Whoever gives me—that is, offers me—as food to those seeking food, speaking through the very nature of food, he indeed approaches me in this manner, as I am truly and imperishably present. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, as for another person who, when the time has come, eats food without first giving it to those in need—him, that man who eats the food, I eat as food itself; I consume him. To this he says: "In that case, I am afraid of liberation, because it entails becoming the Self of all. Let there be only the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), for even if I am liberated, I would still be food and thus subject to being eaten. [The Teacher replies: "Do not fear this, for eating all desires is within the scope of conventional worldly discourse."

Having transcended through knowledge this sphere of conventional worldly activity—characterized by the eater and the food and so forth, which is produced by ignorance—the wise man attains the state of Brahman. For him, there exists no second thing that is a separate entity from which he might fear; therefore, there is no cause for fear of liberation. If this is so, then why does he say, "I am the food, I am the eater"? It is said in reply: this conventional activity characterized by the eater and the food is merely a product of worldly convention (*saṃvyavahāra*); it is not an ultimate reality.

Although he is thus constituted, since that which is characterized by Brahman does not exist apart from Brahman, this is stated for the purpose of praising the state of being Brahman—which is the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman: "I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food," and so forth. Therefore, even the slightest trace of defects such as fear, which are caused by ignorance, does not exist for one who has become Brahman through the destruction of ignorance.

I have transcended—that is, I surpass with my supreme sovereign nature—the entire universe (*viśvam*), which is to be honored by all beings beginning with Brahmā; for "universe" (*bhuvanam*) means that in which beings (*bhūtāni*) exist. My light is "suvar," meaning the sun; the letter *na* is used in the sense of comparison. Thus, my light—meaning my radiance—is like the sun, shining once and for all.

Thus, this is the supreme knowledge of the Self (paramātma-jñāna) established by the two Vallīs; having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, and having undertaken great austerity like Bhṛgu, he who knows this Upaniṣad as it has been described—his fruit is liberation as previously stated.
Om. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with great vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we never harbor mutual hatred. Om. Peace! Peace! Peace!

Thus ends the commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the wandering ascetic teacher (parivrājaka-ācārya) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda.
